speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, until the very last minutes of the debate yesterday evening it was not my intention to exercise my right of reply. The debate has, I think, been rather illuminating, conducted on a high plane, and I am quite willing to let the people of Canada decide as to the merits of the respective contentions which have been presented to the house. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), however, in his address last night made use of certain language and made certain statements which I cannot leave unanswered or unchallenged. He opened his remarks by reading a quotation from Professor Kennedy to the effect that a question like this should always be discussed free from all political leanings or partisanship, but I am compelled to say that my hon. friend did not follow that advice with conspicuous devotion. His first words were rather for the purpose of trying to belittle and even to throw ridicule upon the work of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and my own modest cooperation in that respect.
I think not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But immediately afterwards he took good care to claim credit for everything that had been achieved by way of constitutional reform for the leaders of the Conservative party. Let me tell my hon. friend that I gladly and enthusiastically commend the work and achievements of Sir Robert Borden in regard to Canadian autonomy and his share in contributing towards building up the imperial structure on a stable and firm basis of equality of status and nationhood. I do so with all the more pleasure because that work stands in striking contrast to, and in glaring contradiction of, the words of the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) and of the leader of the opposition himself. Listen to the language of the resolution adopted by the

Shipping Legislation-Mr. Lapointe
Imperial War conference of 1917 of which Sir Robert Borden was a leading member:
The Imperial WTar conference are of opinion that the readjustment of the constitutional relations of the component parts of the empire is too important and intricate a subject to be dealt with during the war, and that it should form the subject of a special imperial conference to be summoned as soon, as possible after the cessation of hostilities.
They deem it their duty, however, to place on record their view that any such adjustment, while thoroughly preserving all existing powers of self-government and complete control of domestic affairs, should be based upon a full recognition of the dominions as autonomous nations

They were not afraid of using that word.

of an imperial commonwealth, and of India as an important portion of the same, should recognize the right of the dominions and India to an adequate voice in foreign policy and in foreign relations, and should provide^ effective arrangements for continuous consultation in all important matters of common imperial concern, and for such necessary concerted action, founded on consultation, as the several governments may determine.
May I quote also these words of Sir Robert Borden in his book, Constitutional Development :
But I have never wavered in the firm and constant belief that, within the British commonwealth of nations, Canada will find her most commanding influence, her widest usefulness, and her highest destiny. With that opinion is coupled a fixed and absolute conviction that the unity of the empire can alone find its expression in complete autonomy and in equality of nationhood. A strong Canadian national spirit is entirely consistent with a firm purpose to maintain our country in a high place within the British commonwealth.
Will the leader of the opposition apply to Sir Robert Borden the words he used towards his successor-
Absolutely.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-for exactly the same language, for the same work? Did Sir Robert Borden let go the mooring? Did he cut the painter? Did he drift away from the little islands, to use the words of my hon. friend? As regards the other men who were associated with him at that Imperial War conference, did Hughes of Australia cut the painter? Did Massey of New Zealand let go the mooring? Did Smuts of South Africa drift from the little islands? As regards those statesmen of the empire who came later in 1926, did Balfour, whose last political work is that great achievement of having coupled his name with that magnificent report of 1926, also let go the mooring? Did Baldwin, Chamberlain, Bruce of Australia, all the prime ministers of the six nations of the empire-and I am proud to
use the word-also cut the painter? Indeed, the only discordant voices have been from some opponents of the Canadian government and I am sorry to have to reach the conclusion that political partisanship seems to have been the main reason of the criticism.
They have not even been in accord with themselves in their attacks. Listen to their objections; read their newspapers and hon. members will see that one school claims that the whole thing is a sham; that nothing has been done; that no change has been effected, while the other school claims that we are on the road to disaster; that revolution is looming ahead of us; that separation is the thing that we should dread. In fact, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George yesterday in the same speech propounded two doctrines. In one part he described the work of 1929 as being futile, infantile, childish, foolish. Really,
I added some words to my vocabulary listening to my hon. friend yesterday. In the next breath he depicted the dangers which were on the horizon of the empire as a result of the work that has been done. That gloomy picture, which I am sorry to say my hon. friend the leader of the opposition also held up, has not even the merit of novelty. At every stage of our constitutional evolution, reactionaries have been seen opposing every reform because, they said, it was leading to separation. Every time, I repeat, the voice of reaction was raised. Yes, every step along the road to self-government was resisted as a step away from the empire and towards separation. When Baldwin and Lafontaine fought in order that parliament should control taxation and expenditure they were described as rebels leading this country to separation from the empire. They were called traitors. Sydenham, Metcalfe and Lord John Russell in their writings all took that stand. Yet who to-day will deny that those men who achieved responsible government in Canada have been the real founders of the British commonwealth? I agree with the suggestion that I heard somewhere that a monument should be erected to Baldwin and Lafontaine at the very door of Downing street because they had been the preservers of the British Empire. The winning of fiscal freedom in 1859, the right of negotiating commercial conventions, the efforts of Edward Blake in 1876 and 1877 to have the instructions to the governor generals of Canada changed in order that they might accord with the status of Canada, the negotiation and the signature of our treaties-all these were viewed with concern by those of that type of mind as manifestations of separatist tendencies. Separation, letting go the moor-

Shipping Legislation-Mr. Lapointe
ings, cutting the painter, drifting away from those little islands-these have always been the words that have been flung in the face of the reformer in this country and elsewhere in the British Empire. Let me illustrate that by a few quotations.
In 1839-I am going back a long way-when the battles were being fought for responsible government in Canada, the select committtee of the legislative council of Upper Canada brought in a report, and listen to this:
After an attentive and disinterested consideration of this subject, your committee are led to the conclusion that the adoption of the plan proposed by the Earl of Durham, in which this (responsible government) is the prominent feature must lead to the overthrow of the great colonial empire of England.
Opposing the Durham report. In 1843, Governor Metcalfe was writing, "the obvious consequence of the concession of responsible government will be separation," and he was saying of Baldwin and Lafontaine, "I regard their faint professions of a desire to perpetuate the connection of the colony with the mother country as utterly worthless."
In 1855, when confederation was looming on the horizon of this country and being discussed in the parliament of the United Kingdom, Mr. Dunkin, in the parliamentary debates, was referring to separation and said:
Sir, I believe in my conscience that this step now proposed-
Mind you, that was confederation:
-is one directly and inevitably tending to this other step; and for that reason-even if I believed, as I do not, that it bids fair to answer ever so well in the other respects-because I am an Englishman and hold to the connection with England, I must be against this scheme.
In 1882, speaking on Edward Blake's motion that Canada should have the power to negotiate commercial agreements with any British possession or foreign state, Sir John A. Macdonald declared:
Disguise it as you will, this means separation and independence.
In 1895, the Colonial Office sent the following despatch:
To give the colonies the power of negotiating treaties for themselves without reference to Her Majesty's government would be to give them an international status as separate and sovereign states, and would be equivalent to breaking up the empire into a number of independent states.
I am free to admit that I am disappointed in my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. After his professions of Canadianism the other day and Canada first, I did not expect that he would indulge in this-shall I say?-distortion 
of the motives of those who have given their best to try to solve the present difficulties and to ensure the maintenance and preservation of our great association on a stable basis. Does he not realize that this is not a unilateral document? It is not the work of Canada alone. It is the combined work of the representatives of Great Britain and the Dominions. Does he not realize that the spirit which inspired them was an earnest desire and a determination to ensure the maintenance and preservation of our great association? Does he not realize that the voice of a group of free nations united by a great bond is more powerful than that of subordinate colonies? Has he not learned from the course of English and Canadian history that the fuller the liberty, the stronger the bond becomes?
I resent deeply, and my hon. friend will pardon me for being frank about it, the implied imputation contained in the words which were used by the leader of the opposition, and I throw back the unworthy suggestion and insinuation. It is that same spirit of resistance which still manifest itself as it has done at every period of our constitutional evolution; but let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, and the people of Canada that the definition of equal status will stand unchanged and unchangeable. By claiming, as my hon. friend did again last night, that the fact that we do not amend our own constitution implies inequality of status, my hon. friend is fighting a rearguard action in the defence of his theories. How is it that those who are responsible for the work that has been done, that those who have been the pioneers, that all those who have worked to achieve reform, are satisfied with this sort of equality, while my hon. friend who is rather putting obstacles in the way is not satisfied? May I refer to one man in Canada, a journalist of prominence, the editor of an important newspaper, who has been in the forefront of the work to achieve the position which Canada holds to-day? I refer to Mr. Dafoe of the Manitoba Free Press. What does Mr. Dafoe say in his journal about this new attitude of my hon. friend? It will be found in the issue of February 28, 1930.
Dispense.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I must impose this upon my hon. friend; if he does not want to listen to it he will have to go away. Mr. Dafoe said:
The Still Obstructive Mr. Bennett
Mr. Bennett still elects to belong to that small and everdwindling minority which concerns itself to find excuses for casting doubt upon the doctrine of constitutional equality between Great Britain and the dominions. The

Shipping Legislation-Mr. Lapointe
movement to establish this condition of equality, which, it should not be forgotten, must be precedent to effective cooperation by the British nations, has not been a party one. When its history comes to be written the name of Sir Robert Borden must stand very high in the list of those to whom credit is due. Indeed, when the movement is completed and the position of Canada as a coequal member of the commonwealth is accepted without question, the Conservative party, by reason of Sir Robert Borden's record, may be expected to claim the whole credit; indeed there have already been indications, as at the convention of the party held in Winnipeg in 1926, of its purpose to advance this claim. But meanwhile the party is so unfortunate as to have a leader who shows, in every reference which he makes to this question, his dislike to the movement and his desire to belittle the development.
Since the Balfour declaration of 1926 a little group of hair-splitters have been trying determinedly but ineffectively to deny the soundness of the constitutional doctrine embodied in that declaration. Their method has been simple enough. It has been boldly to deny that there is equality; to declare that the explicit statements of the 1926 report are without foundation; and to point to existing anomalies in suport of their contention. Prof. Berriedale Keith is the chief of these critics. Prof. Philip Noel Baker, of London University and a member of the present British parliament, deals very effectively with Dr. Keith and his associates in his recently published book, "The Present Judicial Status of the British Dominions in International Law." Meeting his arguments point by point, Prof Keith says it is impossible to accept his conclusions. In noting those who have associated themselves wth Dr. Keith in fighting this rearguard action, Prof. Baker includes the name of but a single public man. It is perhaps needless to say that the person thus referred to is our Mr. Bennett. Thus Prof. Baker says (page 140):
"The leader of the Conservative opposition in the Canadian House of Commons, Mr. Bennett, has made several speeches in which he has used similar language (i.e., language similar to Keith's), e.g., 'Equality of status was a high-sounding phrase, but it could not properly represent the existing position,' and he deprecated the continued use of wrong nomenclature."
It is therefore characteristic of Mr. Bennett that, having had most of his case against "equality" knocked out by the recommendations of the constitutional committee, he should, in place of accepting graciously this new way of escape from an impossible position, look around frantically for some new pretext for contending that our talk about dominion status is all moonshine, the real position being that we are still in a relation of colonial subordination. Hence his gleeful discovery, as announced in his contribution to the debate on the address, that any claim that Canada has constitutional equality with Great Britain is negatived by the fact that the Dominion parliament has not been vested with power to amend the Canadian constitution at will. The reply to this is quite simple and effective. The British parliament is not willingly retaining any control over our constitution; it is ready to turn a responsibility, which would be irksome and dangerous
if it were called upon to exercise it, over to Canadian jurisdiction if the Dominion and the provinces can agree among themselves as to the methods by which the constitution is to be amended. The fact upon which Mr. Bennett seizes so hopefully relates to a purely domestic matter for which a domestic solution must be sought.
Are the Conservatives of Canada willing to have Mr. Bennett tie them up definitely to an attitude of unenlightened opposition to a constitutional development, already achieved, which is acceptable to the vast majority of Canadian people? This ungracious, stubborn attitude by Mr. Bennett towards the national status which Canada has achieved by grace of the combined efforts of public men of all parties is very tiresome to the great mass of the people of Canada, and it must be exasperating to most of his colleagues, who would doubtless be much happier in taking credit to themselves and their party for the constitutional progress that has been made.
So, as I stated, those who have worked to achieve the result which has been reached are satisfied with the present position, and I cannot understand why my hon. friend should still raise this question as implying inequality.
Fears were expressed by both the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George and the leader of the opposition with regard to what may happen concerning Canadian navigation and shipping. My hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George says that it means the sweeping away of legislation. It does not mean anything of the kind. It means the right to enact our own legislation. It means that we, as is stated in the report, want willingly to cooperate on all subjects where cooperation and concerted action are desirable. That will be done. Why distrust the people of Canada? Why distrust the parliament of Canada? The fact that we have the power of a self-governing country in shipping and navigation as well as in other spheres of legislation does not mean that we are going to exercise that power foolishly. Self-government, as I said yesterday, implies trust. Surely my hon. friend is not serious when he thinks that the first use that the parliament of Canada will make of the right of legislation will be to sweep away all the statutes which have been useful to Canadian shipping and navigation. The only change that is effected is a change from subordination to cooperation, from conflict to harmony. That is the change that is being made. My friend said: Let us proceed slowly in this matter. Then a few minutes later he blamed the government for having brought up this resolution at this late hour of the session. He says we are proceeding too fast, he beseeches us to proceed slowly, and afterward he blames us for

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, but apparently we should proceed slowly.
In the last part of his remarks-and it will be the last of mine-my hon. friend lectured the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson) and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and I suppose, indirectly, myself, for using the word "nation" in the description of Canada. Well, surely this will be astounding news to the Canadian people. They have heard the word used by all their leaders for a number of years, certainly long prior to the conference of 1926.	My friends from Bow River and
Winnipeg are certainly in good company. I should like my hon. friend to peruse this work of Sir Robert Borden, his former leader. The word " nation " is the only one which is used by him to express what Canada is among the countries of the world. Shall I quote a few sentences? I think it is useless, but the word appears on every page. My hon. friend referred to the legal meaning which may be attached to it, and he says that the word should not be used. Will hon. members permit me to quote the words of the Hon. Charles Doherty, who was Minister of Justice during the whole term of the Borden government? Hon. members will find these words quoted in Hansard of 1927 at page 1703:
It has not been claimed on this side of the house that this treaty-
Meaning the peace treaty.
-made Canada a nation; nor has it been claimed that anything that happened at the Peace conference made Canada a nation. Canada has grown to nationhood and Canada is a nation; and she does not go seeking anywhere to any of the allied or associated powers, to any foreign power, to Great Britain herself, to the entire Peace conference, to confer upon her the gift of nationhood.
Later in the excerpt I find:
Nationhood is a matter of fact; it is not a question of what is written in a statute book or what is declared by one nation in relation to another.
Then at a later time he stated:
I have referred to the recent discussion with regard to the aviation law. Over in Great Britain they recognize our national status and

that constitutionally the whole field of government of Canada is ours. It is only in this country that you find the little man -who wants to hang on to the colonial status of his country and to insist that she is subordinate to and to be governed by another portion of the empire. However great that portion may be-and we all respect it, we all recognize what she was the source of for us all, and we shall all be happy to recognize her as the first among these equal nations-we contend that, as a matter of fact, we stand as an equal nation within the empire.

May I ask a question?
Does the hon. gentleman remember that after the Minister of Finance made his speech on the budget the words "Canadian nation" came from the 'Lips of the leader of the opposition, but they were not recorded in Hansard the day after?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I could mention many similar statements indeed. If the rules of the house would permit me I would mention a statement contained in a message sent to the people of Canada on the sixtieth anniversary of confederation. All those high authorities surely did not want to let go the moorings; they did not want to Cut the painter; they did not want to drift away from the little islands in the North sea, as my hon. friend so eloquently stated last night.
Canada is a nation; she may hold her head high because of the part she .played in the world war and because of her work in all national, political, social and international fields, because of her sacrifice and because of the respect in which she is held by all foreign nations. Canada is a nation; she will not recognize those who refuse to work with her on terms of nationhood; she will not permit them to shape the thoughts and the policies of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I did not
desire to interrupt the remarks of the hon. gentleman, but he must have known that he put the wrong interpretation upon one observation I -made. As he knows, I was referring to the legal definition of the term " nation," and he also knows that the authorities are clear that there can be no nation, in the sense in which it is judicially interpreted, unless it be an independent sovereignty. My hon. friend knows as a matter of law that my contention is correct; I used the word nation just as he used it and as we use it frequently -in the colloquial sense. The judicial interpretation is and always has been that there can be no such thing as a nation, either in internatlional law or domestic law, unless there be a sovereignty.

Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that a resolution and humble address be presented to His Most Excellent Majesty the King, in the following words:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the (Senate and) Commons of Canada in parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty praying that you may graciously be pleased to give your consent to submitting a measure to the parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and northern Ireland to amend the British North America acts. 1867 to 1916, the four agreements in the schedule hereto set out being scheduled to such act and the said act being expressed as follows or to the following effect:
An Act to Amend the British North America Acte, 1867 to 1916
Whereas the four several agreements in the schedule set out were entered into between the government of the Dominion of Canada and the governments of Manitoba, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan respectively on the dates which the said several agreements respectively bear;
And whereas each of the said agreements has been approved by the parliament of Canada and by the legislature of the province to which it relates;
And whereas subsequently to the execution of the agreement with the province of Alberta it was agreed that in addition to the rights accruing thereunder to the said province, it should be entitled to such further rights, if any. with respect to the subject matter of the said agreement as were required to be vested in the province in order that it might enjoy rights equal to those confered upon or reserved to the province of Saskatchewan under any agreement upon a like subject matter thereafter approved and confirmed in the same manner as the said agreement with the prov- . inee of Alberta, and provision accordingly was made by the parliament of Canada and by the legislature of the province;
And whereas each of the said agreements provides that the same shall come into force only after it has been confirmed by this parliament, and the Dominion of Canada has requested and consented to the enactment of this act;
Be it enacted by the King's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the lords spiritual and temporal, and commons, in this present parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows:
1.	The said several agreements are hereby confirmed and shall have the force of law respectively notwithstanding anything in the British North America acts, 1867 to 1916, or any order in council or terms or conditions of 2419-166
union made or approved under any of the said acts, or in any act of parliament of Canada.
2.	The agreement with the province of Alberta in the schedule hereto contained shall have the force of law as aforesaid, subject to the proviso that in addition to the rights accruing thereunder to the said province, the said province shall be entitled to such further rights, if any, with respect to the subject matter of the said agreement as are required to be vested in the said province in order that it may enjoy rights equal to those which may be conferred upon or reserved to the province of Saskatchewan under agreement with such last mentioned province in the schedule hereto contained.
3.	This act may be cited as the "British North America Act, 1930" and the British North America acts, 1867 to 1916. and this act may be cited together as the "British North America acts, 1S67 to 1930."
All of which we humbly pray Your Majesty to take into Your favourable and gracious consideration.
He said:	The purpose of this address is
apparent from the text. It is to ask the British parliament to confirm and thereby give force and effect to the agreements which have been entered into between the government of Canada and the legislatures of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. These several agreements have been approved by this parliament and by the several legislatures I have mentioned. They have been approved, without a division, by both houses of this parliament and for that reason I think it unnecessary at this moment to do more than indicate the purpose of the address in order to express the belief that it too will be passed with like unanimity.
My hon. friends will realize that at the moment we are amending the British North America Act; in other words, Canada is now engaged in the process of amending her own constitution in so far as that step has become necessary under the agreements into which she has entered. The part played by the parliament at Westminster is at the instance of this parliament; the parliament at Westminster lends its good offices, so to speak, to enact what in accordance with our method of proceeding is essential to give force and effect to the agreements. That, however, in no way lessens the significance of the amendment of the constitution being our own amendment and made in accordance with our established method of procedure. The parliament at Westminster, of its own initiative, would never think of attempting to make an amendment to our constitution. It acts in these matters as an agent of the government of Canada.

That is what we are asking them to do, and that coincides exactly with the remarks I made yesterday. Hon. gentlemen will notice that the legislation we are asking the British parliament to pass is in these words:
Be it enacted by the King's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the lords spiritual and temporal, and commons, in this present parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows:
So far as I know the Lords Spiritual and Temporal hold office in Great Britain, not in Canada. The House of Commons that is referred to is the House of Commons sitting in Great Britain. So we now have complete and absolute proof upon the records of this parliament that by the constitutional changes that give us so-called equality of status we cannot amend our own constitution as can Australia, as can South Africa and as can Great Britain itself. That is the story.
I find it difficult to understand the warmth with which the Minister of Justice was dealing with this phase of the matter when he was considering another subject, but let there be no misunderstanding. Surely hon. members opposite do not insult the intelligence of the ordinary man on the street by asking him to believe there is an equality when the word "equality" means just what it says, the power to do the same thing, and we have not the power to do the same thing as England does, as Australia does and as South Africa does in the manner and form by their constitutions prescribed, which I will not take time to discuss at present.

We are solemnly sitting here, the elected members of the House of Commons, asking by petition of this house and the Senate that the parliament of Great Britain may be pleased to act as we request, and at the close of the petition we find these words:
All of which we humbly pray Your Majesty to take into your favourable and gracious consideration.
That is, we are asking that a parliament three thousand miles away may be pleased to do it. Suppose no one introduces the measure; then what happens? Suppose no one in the parliament of Great Britain introduces this matter into the House of Commons or the House of Lords. What is the result? The Minister of Justice will make a speech on equality of status, and in perfervid eloquence declare to the Canadian people that this is so or it is not so because he, the Minister of Justice, has said so. I do say this to the minister:	It is just such observations as have
been made here this morning and as the Prime Minister has made about the equality of status of Canada, when it is not so, that make Canadians question the sincerity of the government in the whole matter, because they are presuming upon the Canadian people when they make that statement. After all, there is some intelligence in Canada and people will not be deluded by observations made by any man, however important he may be, when he says things are equal when they are not equal. You cannot do it that way.
It is true that the British parliament will do as this parliament asks, or at least we assume that to be so, but supposing they do not do so? Who is going to introduce your bills? Someone must do it; someone in that parliament must take the responsibility of seeing that the bills are introduced and passed, that a majority is secured in their favour and that they are enacted, and all the sophistry in the world, all the casuistry in the world cannot get away from the fact that to amend our constitution, to give validity to the transfer of the resources to western Canada, to make legal that which is now illegal, we have to go to a parliament three thousand miles away. You cannot get away from it. It is a significant circumstance that on the same morning when a minister of the crown solemnly declares that there is equality of status between Great Britain and Canada, within the next few minutes the Prime Minister of the country moves that a humble petition be sent to His

B.N.A. Act-Natural Resources
Majesty the King, praying that he have his parliament at Westminster enact legislation to give validity, life and form to something which to-day is not worth the paper on which it is written, because we have not the power to do that which we have done, and are now seeking ratification of the Imperial parliament. That is what causes distrust of the whole action of the government; that is what makes people ask, "What does this mean, when men go about and talk in these terms about equality when they know there is none, when they know that the essence of nationhood is the right to amend its own constitution." Why the attempt to deceive; why not at once say frankly that we use these words in the broad and colloquial sense? We know that as a matter of law this is not so; we know that any court that might consider the question would have to decide otherwise; we know what the legal position is, but we use these terms as I have used them from my youth in referring to Canada as a "nation," referring to the "status" and referring to these matters in that sense. When, as yesterday and this morning, we are dealing with matters which touch legal questions, then precedents, authorities and judgments govern, and you cannot give to words meanings they do not legally possess in order to attach significance to a phrase which will not bear judicial interpretation in the sense suggested.
That is the reason I said to the minister what I did say in connection with this matter some days ago. I gravely doubt whether we should proceed in this way. Once more I venture to fight a rearguard action, in the language of the Minister of Justice, when I point out to him that it has not been customary to deal with constitutional matters in this way. Constitutional matters usually have been dealt with in the form of a statute which embodies the arrangement or agreement which has been entered into. It was so in the original British North America Act, and it has been so in the different amendments which have been made to that act. We are now ratifying agreements, but part of those agreements require no ratification. I put this to the Minister of Justice as a suggestion which I think he, as a lawyer, will regard as important: If we make the agreements in question a part of our constitution when portions of the agreements require no confirmation because they deal with purely domestic matters, but do they not hereafter become a part of the constitution, and are they not only amendable in the manner in 2419-166J
which the constitution can be amended? There is a section in the agreements which declares that any matter referred to in the agreements may be dealt with by an understanding between the parties concerned, that is, between Alberta and the Dominion, between Saskatchewan and the Dominion and between Manitoba and the Dominion. But that only refers, as I take it, to limited portions of the agreements and if the hon. gentleman will look at them he will see that the limitations to which I refer are thus expressed. I will say this, that not before in the history of British institutions has a constitutional change been made by the confirmation of agreements; such changes have heretofore been embodied in legislation, as in the Manitoba Act. The government takes the responsibility in this matter; the Minister of Justice, the chief law officer of the crown, is satisfied in that regard and therefore the motherland. Now I am merely speaking as a member of parliament, not in any sense as the leader of a party; I am making a suggestion to him as one lawyer to another. I suggest that this is not the way in which it has been done.
Just here I might point out one other matter. Those who read history and endeavour to form conclusions and draw inferences all realize that a day, a year, or fifty years in the life of a state are as nothing; all we can do is to endeavour as best we can to conclude that certain things done to-day will, years hence, have a result which we believe will be injurious or beneficial to the body politic. The immediate consequences are not of concern; what is of vital concern is the effect upon the body politic in the years that are to come, and in that regard I have some measure of pride and satisfaction in looking back upon the rearguard actions I have fought, for, by a strange circumstance, the results which I predicted would come about in connection with what has been done have usually occurred. I know not why that is so; I only know that has been the case. When I ventured, twenty-five years ago, to point out in connection with these resources what the inevitable result would be, I can remember one of the friends of my hon. friends saying, "We have heard the last of you. This country is going to have the money, and the resources are nothing." When I remember the vociferous cheers of those hon. gentlemen in those days; when I recall the scoffing and the scorn which they expressed, for our demand that the new prov-

B.N.A. Act-Natural Resources
inces should be granted their resources I take some pride and satisfaction in thinking that where the vanguard camps to-day the rear will march to-morrow.

I cannot agree with

The British North America Act first received the assent of all the provinces, and I submit that the forwarding of this petition by this parliament does not represent the views of the provinces in the sense that it is expressing the acquiescence and concurrence of the provinces concerned. Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to delay these proceedings, but I feel that I should reiterate what I said when the agreements were before the house. After an agreement had been concluded with the province of Alberta, satisfactory both to the Dominion of Canada and to the province, the government of Saskatchewan succeeded in wresting from this government more favourable terms; and we now ask the British parliament to adopt legislation by which the province of Alberta will be given something which it has not asked for. That shows the weakness of the posi-

B.NA. Act-Natural Resources
tion which was created by this government agreeing to give to Saskatchewan something more than Alberta had asked for, and something more than I think was necessary. That is my first objection.
My second objection is that a wrong principle is introduced herein. It is a wrong policy to introduce into an agreement the principle introduced herein, that an act enacted by this parliament, even though reenacted or ratified by the British parliament, shall not be final. We thus open the way for litigation upon the agreements which we have concluded.
I think also there is something in the point raised by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLaren). I would remind him and the other representatives from the maritime provinces that at all times they have my deepest sympathy, because I think those provinces have been made the victims of confederation. [DOT] However, I remind him also of the very lucid interpretation which was put upon the constitution by Lord Haldane. I do not remember the particular case-I am sure the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) would remember it-but it originated in Australia. His Lordship made an extremely interesting, and from my humble layman's point of view, a most conclusive comparison as between the constitutions of Australia, Canada and South Africa. He pointed out how mistaken many Canadians are in referring to the British North America Act as a contract, when in fact it was only the result of a contract. The old colonies agreed to renounce their existence, they laid down the terms under which they were prepared to enter into confederation in the form of provinces, and they sent that contract to London; but there it was amended greatly by the various representatives of those colonies, and finally the British parliament passed a statute which differed from both the contract passed in Quebec and the London treaty.

I admit that, but nevertheless-and I think this was Lord Haldane's conclusion, and I believe it was right-once that law was passed, the old colonies lost their identity-they became provinces under the new law, just as the Dominion was created under the same new law. The powers of each are defined by the statute itself, and no further reference can be made to the contract as against the letter and spirit of the constitution itself. Of course, history records how both the contract and the legislation were imposed upon the people of the maritime provinces; and I quite realize they should be very sensitive in regard to anything which may look to them as a further abandonment of what they claim as their rights. But in regard to this I think the way is quite clear. The government of any of those provinces can have representatives before the British parliament and make such opposition to the enactment of these agreements as it may think fit. It may plead before the committee of the House of Commons in England what it considers to be an abridgement of its rights or claims in equity, as they were presented here during the debate on the agreements. That can be done; but I do not think we could agree in this house to renounce our right to make an agreement with various provinces upon matters concerning only those provinces, afterwards asking ratification by the British parliament in concurrence with the provinces immediately interested. Any individual, so far as that is concerned, may go before the British parliament and have his views presented to that body as against these agreements or any amendment of the constitution.
This brings me to the point made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), and I think it is worth while looking into it also. There is no doubt something rather ludicrous in the contrast between the debates that have preceded, on the national status of Canada, and the debate on this motion. There is not the slightest doubt that so long as we submit to the exercise of imperial jurisdiction over our constitution, or upon any agreement that we may make with the provinces or with one or more of the provinces, it is absurd to talk of Canada having attained her full national status. But where I think the solution is to be found is in the comparison between two very simple words, that is, the word "right" and the word "power." Undoubtedly the leader of the opposition is quite right as a lawyer when he says that so long as we do not exercise the power of amending the constitution, there is something childish and ludicrous in our parading our title as a nation. This looks very much like a boy who would catch hold of his father's military uniform and sword and parade himself as a general because his father, being a general, has received from his commander a military uniform, a plumed hat and a sword.

Is it not against the

Mr. BOURASSA; I am not characterizing the Minister of Justice. I am characterizing the Canadian nation, whether it be the Minister of Justice, Sir Robert Borden or myself, because I have spoken very often concerning the matter. I admit there is something childish in our attitude, but at the same time it is by repeating it that one of these days we shall make good our rights. That is what I come back to. In a previous debate, I think at the opening of this parliament-and I do not want to refer to a past debate except by way of illustration-the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) put the matter quite clearly when he said in effect-and it has been stated time and again outside the house also, and quite rightly:-we have not yet chosen to exercise our undoubted right to amend our constitution according, of course, to the spirit under which it was framed, that is, after agreeing with the provinces as to the manner in which those powers which belong to both jurisdictions or those which belong to only one of them, should be treated. After we have agreed with them, it remains with ourselves to take action, and nobody in England would contradict or interfere, not even Mr. Keith. In Mr. Keith's latest book there is a somewhat melancholy but very clear admission that in the conference of 1926 and in the last conference of 1929 we have made much headway. There is not the slightest doubt that the day the parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures would assert their will to exercise their right of amending their constitution without going to Westminster, no word would be uttered in London against that action. Further, it would not take long before we made our position good before the Imperial parliament as regards the exercise of that power. I remember an opinion expressed as far back as twenty-eight years ago, I think it was, again by Lord Haldane, when he said that it was becoming clearer and clearer every day that in regard to passing legislation at the request of the various colonial legislatures as they were still called, it was realized that the Imperial parliament was exercising a mere power of trusteeship and had nothing to do but to legislate in the manner suggested by those various parliaments.

may arise: supposing the governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, at the next session of the Imperial parliament, when this legislation comes up, make solemn protest against the passing of the legislation; supposing they convince a majority of the members of the Imperial parliament that this agreement is doing an injustice to the people of the maritime provinces: would anybody deny that the Imperial parliament would have both the right and the power to decide as between the claim of Canada in conjunction with Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia, and the counter claims of the maritime provinces?

Not a constitutional

subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF AGREEMENTS FOR TRANSFER OF NATURAL RESOURCES TO WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Why? Supposing the
governments of the maritime provinces demonstrate that, while they have not any possible access to those natural resources which were or which at least some people hold to have been the property of the people of Canada, the parliament of Canada is divesting itself of the rest of those resources after having handed over a large portion of them to Ontario and Quebec without an inch of territory being given to the maritime provinces; supposing the maritime provinces make their claim in equity before the Imperial parliament: will anyone deny that the Imperial parliament will have both the right and the power to say that as regards these agreements, especially after we have handed over to Quebec and Ontario such a large portion of those territories, the legislation should not pass until we have compensated the maritime provinces? I do not say that this should be done as a matter of equity, but I say that the British parliament would certainly have a right to say: So long as the people of Canada, through their various political powers, federal and provincial, have not chosen to exercise to the full their right of sovereignty over their constitution; so long as they choose to make us the final legislative arbiters, so to speak, in such matters, we have to consider Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island just as much as Alberta, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, and just as much as the Dominion of Canada. So long as we rely upon the final exercise of legislative power by the Imperial parliament, surely we must be prepared to expect from that parliament the exercise of a duty which we would ourselves have to exercise if we had to decide between two or three different contentions presented to us by governments, corporations or individuals.

B.N.A. Act-Natural Resources
I repeat, I am not making these remarks to obstruct or retard the passage of this measure, but I am afraid that in the last few years we have developed the habit of giving a great deal of time to comparatively small questions and questions of money, and then leaving till the last two or three days of the session the greatest questions of state which should be most carefully considered because their consequences in the future may be very far-reaching, either as regards the relations between the Dominion and the provinces or the relations between the various provinces themselves. I thought it was my duty to suggest that the question was not so simple as it has been regarded; but at the same time I would not like to put myself along the same line of thought adopted by the hon. leader of the opposition, who seems to consider that this question of constitutional amendments is one that we cannot solve. We can solve it. We can exercise our rights, and therefore we can make the power in conformity with the right, make the fact conform with the theory. But so long as we have not done it, so long as for reasons good or bad, such as have been expressed time and again, by the premier of Quebec, Mr. Taschereau, whose views I respect but do not share-so long as you have people east and west who imagine that Canada is not just enough, that Canada is not manly enough, to exercise its nationhood to the full, that we must rely upon a foreign tribunal to pass final adjudication upon our legal quarrels, upon a foreign parliament to give the final touch to our most important pieces of legislation, then we must be prepared to accept some of the consequences, nay, all the consequences, of that state of fact which wisely or unwisely we choose to keep in being.
That was suggested to me partly by the argument made by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLaren). We of the west or of the central parts of Canada, are too apt to forget the dire position in which the maritime provinces find themselves. They have been, I repeat, the victims of confederation. They have paid practically all the penalties of the confederation pact, with very little compensation; and as far as I am concerned I would view with sympathy some means being taken by those provinces to assert their rights. I suggest humbly and in a friendly way to my friends of the maritime provinces-I think they know the sincerity of my feelings-that they should induce their provincial governments to take direct action and send their delegates to London to place
their views before the Imperial parliament. They would then have at once the advantage of having their views properly aired and, as well, a declaration by the Imperial parliament as to whether that body still considers itself as the arbiter between the various provinces of Canada, or as between the Dominion and those provinces.

speechtext: I want to join with the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLaren) in protesting against this legislation going through until the question is decided whether or not the maritime provinces have any right to those lands. They claim that they have. They may be wrong. Their claim is opposed by our friends from the west. I say that that claim should be determined before this thing passes irrevocably out of our hands. The present assurances do not go far enough. They are the same assurances that were given to our representatives in 1912, that when the matter came to be discussed and the lands were given over to the western provinces, the claims of the maritime provinces would be recognized. That time has come and those claims have not been recognized. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) has enlarged on the point that I had in my mind, that it will be the duty of the three maritime governments to appear before the Imperial parliament and oppose the passage of this legislation until that claim is settled one way or the other. It may be that we have no claim. Very well; let us have it decided; and then the people of the maritimes will be satisfied. But until that question is settled I believe that the people of the maritime provinces will feel that they have been unjustly treated in this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: I have just indicated one important change-the closed season has been extended by fifteen days. The present treaty embodies a number of the recommendations of the joint fisheries commission. These recommendations had been approved by order in council so far as Canada is concerned, but to meet the desires of the United States government in the matter of sufficient authority they have now been put in the form of a treaty.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last summer when I had an opportunity to visit Prince Rupert I went down to the boats and observed the operations in connection with the landing of the halibut catch and its treatment in cold storage for the purpose of ascertaining something in connection with the industry. The truth is that the fish are being absolutely destroyed. I found that halibut do not attain a reasonable size until their seventh or eighth year; some live to an age of thirty-five or forty years. Formerly halibut were caught weighing over four hundred pounds. Now the halibut from the open sea are being caught, brought into port and shipped in bond to the United States, principally to Boston, and this affords considerable traffic for the railways. Our fishermen get for their halibut a smaller price than the Americans get for their catch because of the duty against the importation of halibut into the United States. That is the basis, I assume, of the suggestion made the other day that there should be a countervailing duty in respect to fish.

Halibut Fisheries Convention
Although I had heard a great deal about it before I went to Prince Rupert, I satisfied myself from the questions which I asked and from what I saw while there that unfortunately heretofore the provisions of the treaty have not been fully observed. In other words, the patrol has been inadequate, and being inadequate has been ineffective. I regret to say the fishermen told me that the industry was really threatened with extinction, and that unless very drastic action were taken to enforce the regulations the result would be extremely serious. I think we realize how desirable it is that the halibut fishing industry in the north Pacific should not be destroyed. Halibut is one of the best food fishes in the world, and it is in constant demand by our friends to the south. The extension of the closed season, I think, from the information I gathered at Prince Rupert, will improve conditions and I only desire to impress upon the government the very great importance of insisting on the regulations under the treaty being respected, and that without fear, favour or affection we should prosecute those who violate them. The member for Skeena (Mr. Brady) placed upon Hansard a year ago-I daresay hon. members will recall the occasion -a story in connection with the enforcement of the treaty regulations. I took the trouble to make some inquiries at the time, because it struck me that if what he related were repeated frequently it would result in the entire extinction of halibut in the northern Pacific.
I welcome this treaty as an advance on the former treaty. I hope the extension of the closed season and the establishment of areas in which no fish shall be taken will to some extent at least meet the difficulty. Under the circumstances I would impress upon the government once more how desirable it is to enforce the law. I am confident they may count upon the support of every Canadian who is interested in this great fishery in seeing that the law is observed and the treaty respected, and that no reasonable expenditure will be too great if it has the effect of maintaining the halibut fishery for posterity.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, permit me to say a few words on this very important treaty. The very fact that two nations decide to enter into a treaty presupposes the importance of the subject matter dealt with. Undoubtedly the halibut fishing industry is of very great importance, not merely to Canada but also to the United States. I have read the treaty as brought down yesterday. I am in perfect accord with the efforts made to conserve the greatest fishing banks at present in the world. If
hon. members have read the story of our Atlantic fishing grounds they will recall that many years ago halibut existed in abundance on the great fishing banks of the North sea; to-day they are non-existent. We find that, steadily, for the last twenty years halibut which was caught in abundance off cape Flattery, many years ago, were decimated in that area, and1 then Hecate straits, became the great centre of our halibut industry and continued to be so for a period of ten to fifteen years. Once more the scene changed. To-day the halibut fishermen have to travel right to the extreme end of Alaskan boundaries; they have to go as far as Kodiak, and beyond, even to Unalaska near the Behring sea. That being the case we must realize the gravity and importance of this treaty renewed between two great nations.
I do regret however that in the text of the treaty the government has overlooked a very important matter in respect to the halibut situation. At the present time the great weight of power, wealth and control of these fisheries is not in Canadian hands and has not been for years past; it is in the hands of Americans. They have the wealth and the power, and through these sources they have obtained almost complete control of this great and important fishing industry. For example, last year in the port of Prince Rupert over 30,000,000 pounds of halibut were landed, and of that poundage 20,000,000 pounds came in American vessels. For some reason or another it is a very easy matter to have the press misrepresent what one is trying honestly to represent to the public. What I said last year, and what I repeat this year, has nothing to do with retaliation upon the United States; it is simply a question of equality and fair dealing between the two countries which have made this treaty. I want to impress upon the government the fact that in our salmon fisheries we have a large area of neutral waters; strictly speaking these should be part of the Canadian waters. I refer to the great Hecate straits lying between Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland of Canada. What happens in connection with this fishing ground? Every year hundreds of American fishing vessels enter our harbours and violate the sacred treaty which was entered into years ago between the United States and Canada. I gave evidence of this last year. The result is that in every phase of this great and important industry the Canadian fisherman has not the rights to which he is entitled, while on the other hand the American nation realize the importance and the greatness of the fishing industry and

Halibut Fisheries Convention
are ever alert to get every advantage. So important is the fishing industry and so great the demand of the American public for fish that we can never hope to supply it. Fish is one of the most important foods consumed by the American people. I may be too late, but I ask the Prime Minister to make one more effort to secure for Canadian fishermen, their rights in connection with this important industry. A few weeks ago, I placed before this house certain facts; they are facts which can be authenticated by any one who desires so to do. Canada has in Prince Rupert a wonderful port on the Pacific coast, and it is the only port at which American vessels can deliver their fish and have them sent with expedition to the great markets of the United States. The result is that the American fishing vessels bring their fish to that port, and they do not pay a single cent; they are charged only one dollar for the licence to fish, and they receive the full benefits of the port. They are allowed to ship their fish from that port in bond; they seek Canadian ports as a shelter from storm; they receive all the benefits we can confer and in return we receive practically nothing.
I urge the government in pursuance of this treaty to try to impress upon the United States the necessity of a fair deal in a matter which has a profound interest both for that country and Canada. That is all I ask.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, may I suggest a method of procedure which might save the time of the committee.
I think the committee on agriculture did excellent work in connection with this bill. The decisions in regard thereto were practically unanimous, indeed I may say absolutely unanimous, but there was just one matter in connection with the bill to which serious objection was taken, and in connection with that matter the minister has agreed to make a statement to the committee. The question to which I refer is the status of the assistant commissioners. Hon. members will recall that a provision was made last year that the assistant commissioner should have all the powers of a commissioner for the purpose of making inquiry, hearing complaints and making decisions. In the original draft of the present bill, which was finally agreed to by the committee, it is intended to take away from the assistant commissioner those powers, and to make him completely subject in every respect to the board and his future powers will depend upon regulations or orders passed by the board. While admitting that this feature from an administrative point of view has considerable merit, and while admitting that a great deal may be said for the change, yet I feel that the producers may not be wholly satisfied. The reason for making the change last year was to give the producer a man with power who would be close to him, a man who could deal effectively and in a speedy manner with any questions which might arise. Personally I believe that the new board will be a good one, will be efficient and will operate excellently, yet I feel that it would have been better if the producers had close to them a man with the pow'ers of a commissioner. If the new board should delegate to these assistant commissioners the full power which they had last year, then my objection would be removed. Before we pass this bill I would like the minister to make a statement in regard to this matter. With that one criticism, I would suggest that considerable time would be saved if the bill were simply passed as a bill and sent forward to its conclusion.

Mr. Chairman, I think
the remarks of the hon., member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) have clearly outlined the objection which he took in the committee when the bill was unanimously passed. Section 10 of the new bill provides:

the commission has power to make inquiry, and any commissioner or assistant commissioner so authorized shall have the same powers as the board might itself have exercised.
The person so authorized would have the same right of inquiry as the board itself. Section 11a of last year's amendment provided :
Each of the assistant commissioners shall have the like powers and duty to receive and investigate complaints and also make investigations without complaint received and make findings thereon, as by the act is given to and imposed upon the board of any commissioner,
Subsection (3) of section 11a of the amendment provides:
There shall be an appeal to the board within fifteen days by any person dissatisfied with a decision of an assistant commissioner.
While the assistant commissioner was given last year the full power to decide for the whole board, of which he was not a member, the individual who might feel that such decision was not a fair one could appeal to the board within fifteen days. I am free to say that the advice offered to me and to the committee in support of section 10 by the chairman of the board and by the legal advisers is that under the amendment, section 11a, the assistant commissioner was given more power that any one of the commissioners. He was given more power than the chairman of 'the board because he could make a finding, whereas no member of the board could do so under the act. Under the new section, which I think we should accept for at least a year's trial, I believe that the recommendations of the assistant commissioner would be more carefully considered because he would know that a finding would -be based thereon. If the assistant commissioner possesed full power with appeal to the board, he might be influenced by a hasty judgment. When he knows that his investigation and his finding require the approval of the board, he will give very careful consideration thereto. Section 10 will provide a greater degree of finality once the case is heard. It does not seem to me that an assistant commissioner would be as careful in making his decision when there was a possibility of the case being reheard by the full board within fifteen days. If the power of making a decision were left with the assistant, many apepals would have to be made to the board, and I think it advisable that the board should have the opportunity to pass upon any matter in which an inquiry is advisable.
As minister of the department charged with the administration of this act through the Board of Grain Commissioners, I want to point out another objection to 11a. Under

subsection 11a of the amendment of last year the department has to supervise two bodies. One body is the Board of Grain Commissioners, headed by a chairman charged with the administration of the act and responsible for decisions made by the assistant commissioner. Inasmuch as these assistant commissioners are appointed not by the governor in council but on the recommendation of the board itself; inasmuch as the three assistant commissioners were chosen for their technical and practical knowledge by the Board of Grain Commissioners, I think it is a very improper situation for these men not to be responsible to the board that engaged them. As regards the three assistant commissioners, one man was taken from the grain trade-I believe he was an elevator operator for the United Grain Growers-and another man, an excellent and well known operator, was taken from the pool. The third man was taken from the Manitoba Agricultural college, on account of his expert knowledge of the whole grain business. I do not think one could criticize the board for their selection of the assistant commissioners, but I do not believe these men selected by the board should be given any more power than any officer of the board. I submit that for the present at least I must take the advice of the officers of the board and ask the committee to accept section 10, which I believe is better than section 11a of the amendment of last year.

I think members of the committee will remember that the other morning when we were speaking of this matter many suggestions were put forward of a much wider character even than those now made by the leader of the opposition as suitable objects for which exemption should be allowed in case of contribution.

In the United States exception is granted on contributions to any corporation or trust or community chest fund, or foundation organized and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, literary or educational purposes, or for the prevention of cruelty to children or animals, but only if no part of the net earnings inures to the benefit of any private shareholder or individual. Distributions to the special fund under the vocational rehabilitation act, authorized by section 7 of that act, posts or organizations of war veterans or auxiliaries, units or societies are also exempt, but only to these posts or organizations if such posts or organizations, funds or societies are organized in the United States or any of its possessions and have no part of their net earnings which inures to the benefit of any private individual. He pointed out the very deplorable conditions prevailing there and said in effect that they were a disgrace. The Reverend Mr. Hamilton also referred to the Robertson commission which was appointed by the present government in 1923. Perhaps I might quote the following recommendations made by that commission in 1924, which recommendations also were submitted to the tariff board. This will be found in the report:
The commission are of the opinion that the hours of labour have been excessively long in some departments of the plant under the two-shift system of operation. The commission recommends that in the interests alike of the company and the workmen, early and earnest attention be given to the elimination of the twenty-four hour change-over period and to the abolition of the seven-day week. The commission recommends that the question of adopting the three-shift plan, eight hours per shift, in the departments of continuous processes, and a maximum of a ten-hour day for the workmen be given the most careful consideration. In our opinion the change would be advantageous to the company and beneficial to the men, and should be adopted.

Why has there been this sudden change since last Wednesday evening? It is very difficult indeed for the average person to understand why the sudden change has taken place. The report was broadcast throughout the length and breadth of this Dominion that the government and the House of Commons as a whole were almost unanimously in favour of doing something to further the acceptance of the eight-hour day. It was felt throughout the land that the House of Commons was in favour of introducing the eight-hour day into the steel mills of this Dominion. Then on Friday evening the leader of the opposition stated from his place in the house that he did not think the resolution was in order, and the Minister of Finance claimed that the idea was impracticable.
_ hundreds of thousands of workingmen in this country are watching with a good deal of interest the action of the government in regard to this particular question. the leader of the government and the opposition were in favour of doing something to inaugurate the eight-hour day in the steel mills of Canada where conditions are in a deplorable state. Mr. Chairman, the bill was

This bill, which is mow

Briefly, section 1 provides a slight amendment to the provisions which was adopted last year in reference to summer residents. Section 1 is to the effect that when an elector is working in one part of a constituency, and has been there long enough to entitle him to vote at that place rather than his usual place of residence, he will be entitled to vote where he is earning his living provided it is in the same constituency. This is to meet a demand made by some of the western members^ and to meet also the requirements of some of the labour people. It will be a convenience not only to the west but to the east, in such places as Seven Islands, in Charfevoix-Mont-morency county, and other places of that kind, as" it will save the voter travelling a very considerable distance to register his vote.
Section 2 lays down rules for a new system which will be adopted in the urban constituencies whereby a double set of enumerators will be used in making up the voters' lists. Last year the act provided for one set of enumerators; this year we have regulations to the effect that there shall be two sets, to make sure the list is as regular and as complete as possible.
Section 3 provides for by-elections. Under the new system inaugurated by the act last year, when a writ of election in any electoral district is issued within six months after a general election there will be no necessity to go through the long process of making up new lists; the lists in the hands of the chief electoral officer at the time will be used for the by-election.
Section 4 provides for the voting of blind men. Representations were made to the committee by blind people to the effect that the present system might be improved, and that a blind man who wishes to vote might be accompanied by a friend who would vouch for him and would also swear that he had
accompanied but one man to the poll. This is now provided for and takes the place of the procedure to which they objected.
Section 5 applies to the constituency of Regina, where instead of providing for eight days between nomination and polling the interval will be fifteen days. I may say that the committee made this recommendation with the understanding that if any other member of the house wishes a similar change in his constituency it will be made now.
Section 6 provides that a legal adviser shall be retained to advise the chief electoral officer in reference to any matter relating to the present election. The idea of the government and of the committee is that Colonel Biggar, who has served as chief electoral officer in former elections, should be retained as legal adviser to his successor.
Section 7 is put forward, in view of the fact that the delay between prorogation and dissolution might be very short, to provide for the necessary changes in order that the regulations for the double set of enumerators will apply in urban centres at the pending election.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering item 3/7a Shall the item carry?

No, Mr Chairman. When the house rose at six o'clock I was discussing the conditions of labour prevailing in the Besco plant at Sydney, and I have one or two other comments to make before we leave this particular item.
The men employed at the steel works at Sydney and for the Besco corporation generally have during the last ten or twelve years gone through several very trying experiences. In 1923 during a bitterly contested strike troops were sent down to Nova Scotia and ultimately the men were forced to go back to work under the same intolerable conditions against which they had so vigorously protested; and they are working under similar conditions at the present time. Several commissions have investigated the industry and in each case they have suggested that immediate improvement be made in the working conditions.
I know it may be said, Mr. Chairman, with a good deal of truth, that the question of labour hours and the general conditions under which the men are engaged in the industry is entirely for the provincial legislature and -t for the federal parliament to deal with. Although recognizing that there is a certain amount of truth in the statement, I cannot altogether agree that the contention as sound.
I think that the parliament of Canada, the supreme legislative body in the Dominion, has a very important duty to perform so far as the conditions of the people are concerned, and I do not think that we as members of this House of Commons are doing the right or proper thing when we attempt to shelve our responsibility in a matter of this character. I know it is very simple indeed for either this parliament or the provincial legislature to say: It is not our responsibility.

But while this dispute between the provincial and federal governments is being settled the working people are getting no particular benefit. Although the question of legislative jurisdiction may be involved, at the present time we are confronted with a concrete situation of some difficulty. This government is being asked to grant certain concessions to an industry, and I say it is not beyond the powers of parliament to say to that industry that parliament will not grant them any such concession unless they are willing to put into effect certain improved conditions in connection with the men they employ. I do not think I am asking too much when I ask parliament to take that action. For the past eight or ten years, perhaps longer than that, the aggrieved men have been looking for some remedy, and up to the present time they have not been accorded it. In the past this parliament has appointed commissions to inquire into social conditions affecting the Canadian people. If parliament has not the right to legislate in connection with social conditions, why do we continue to appoint commissions for the purpose of inquiring into them? I do not think we should tell the working people that we have nothing to say as to the conditions under which men and women are employed in industry. I think I am correct in saying that Practically every hon. gentleman in this house, whether he be on one side or the other, is opposed to the intolerable conditions which prevail in the Besco mills at Sydney, Nova Scotia. If such is the case, if we are unanimous, and if the expressions of opinion on the part of the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition last IVednesday evening are a criterion of the feeling of the men who sit behind those hon. gentlemen, is it beyond the wit of this parliament to devise ways and means to withhold from the iron and steel industry any increased tariff benefits until something is done by the industry to improve the conditions of the workers under its control? I do not think so.
As I said prior to the adjournment, as a result of the statement made by the Prime Minister, and the very concrete and definite, suggestion made by the leader of the opposition within the last few days, the men have been led to believe that this House of Commons is ready to do something for them. But lo and behold, within a few days after those statements are made we are told that parliament is impotent to act in connection with this matter! What will the men say? What will be the average man's reaction to a situation of that kind? He will say that this
