government is not impotent when it comes to doing something for the directors and shareholders of a corporation, but that it is impotent in respest to the interests of the men employed by that concern. To my mind that is a very unfortunate impression to be broadcast throughout the length and breadth of this country. Parliament should not allow the impression to go out that it does not wish to do anything to better the conditions of the most oppressed men in our Dominion. It is an attitude of that character which brings parliament into disrepute. Parliament has functions to perform, and here we have an opportunity to do something in the interests of the men engaged in the steel industry.
We have been asked to give certain valuable concessions to the shareholders and bondholders of the British Empire Steel Corporation. I think I am correct when I say that a very large percentage of those who own bonds and stocks in the steel industries of this country do not live in the Dominion of Canada. In other words, we are going to give valuable concessions to men who are not Canadians, who live outside of Canada, yet it is suggested that we cannot do a thing for men of our own kith and kin engaged in the steel industry. That is why I have risen on these occasions and have protested against any aid being given to the steel corporations until first of all we have it understood that something will be done for the men employed in the steel industry.

I wish to
congratulate the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) and his colleague for having brought to the attention of this house the dissatisfaction of the workers in the steel plants at Sydney and in other parts of the Dominion. He has made special reference to the employees in the plant of the British Empire Steel Corporation, and I believe properly so.
I remember very well the first speech I had the honour to make in this house. It was in the year 1922, and on that occasion I spoke on behalf of the very men whose case has been so ably championed by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. The men in the steel industry had passed through an appalling period of depression and strife. Shocking conditions of intense misery and destitution were depicted before the house. There have been some improvements since that time, but now, on May 27, 1930, we hear another appeal from the steel workers, and perhaps from the miners, for improved and reasonable working conditions. They ask for fair working hours and fair wages, and 2419-169

We are dealing with specific increases in the tariff concerning the steel industry. Let us turn for a moment to the condition of the industry. I have in my hand a Canadian Press despatch dated at Montreal, April 21, 1930,-a month and six days ago. I shall read it for the information of hon. members:

And so on. The steel industry in this country has shown handsome profits and operating surpluses. At this time the country is asked through parliament to give to the shareholders and bondholders in the iron and steel industries an additional opportunity to make greater profits. Will the government which is proposing to grant these great privileges, increases of from 66 per cent to 80 per cent, to this industry, refuse to heed the just appeal of labour? Is labour not to get its share of this improved condition? There was a time, I remember, not so long ago when we used to refer to the hon. gentlemen who sit to the left of the Speaker and to my right as being the friends of the manufacturers. They were pilloried all over the hustings of this country as the friends of the manufacturers, the gentlemen who extended special privileges to their own friends. Not only that, but they frequently argued in response. "Oh, no, we want protection in order to protect the worker." Now we find this government adopting the same principle of protection, and for whom? Are they going to place themselves in the same position as hon. gentlemen to my right have been placed for so many years, as friends of the manufacturers and not friends of the workers? That is the issue, clear cut, which is before us in this house to-night. Are we going to befriend only industries which already make handsome profits, and are we going to leave labour to its own devices, to solve its own problems as best it may without extending to labour any reasonable opportunity to make better the conditions under which it exists? Why, Mr. Chairman, if that be the condition *which we have reached in our political life in Canada to-day, I say we might as well have the Tories in office as have the Liberals in office.
Oh, no.
No, it is not as bad as that.
I say in connection with this particular point that we might as well have the Tories in office as have the Liberals in office.
You are losing faith, man.
Faith in whom?
In yourself of course.

Not in my hon. friend, certainly; I never had much faith in his ability to do anything for Liberalism.

Mr. McINTOSH Why apply that limitation to yourself?

Protection we are told, is to protect labour; we have heard that so frequently from my hon. friends to my right. They have repeated that phrase so often, that protection is to help labour, and we have time and again said to them, "Can you show us that it will help labour or save the consumer from additional costs? I well remember Right Hon. Arthur Meighen standing in his place and saying that protection did not necessarily increase the price to the consumer, and that if he went into office he would see to it that it did not increase the price to the consumer. He said in effect that he was going to protect the working people. Hon. gentlemen to my right always have said that, and tonight we have an opportunity to justify Mr. Meighen's contention and the contention of his friends who still sit in this house. Protection is a privilege which is extended by the Dominion to certain industries; it is a privilege that is eagerly sought by manufacturers and corporations everywhere. It is a privilege which extends to them the opportunity to sell their products to the people in a sheltered market at a higher price than they would bring if they were sold in open competition. The manufacturers seek that privilege eagerly, but they have never to my knowledge handed back in the aggregate to the workers or to the consumers the benefits which they have received by virtue of the protective tariff.
If you want one illustration in that regard all you have to do is to take the textile industry-and it is only an illustration; that is my excuse for introducing it into this discussion The textile" industry is like the steel industry; one enjoys a protection of something over 30 per cent and the other enjoys an even higher protection, yet in the textile industry we have the lowest average weekly wage in any industry in the Dominion of Canada. It is one of the most highly protected industries we have. No longer can hon. gentlemen delude the worker or the common consuming public in this country-
Or anyone else.

-or anyone else by saying that protection will help the worker. Surely, Mr. Chairman, it is not too much to ask that this government, this parliament which has the power to grant these privileges, shall also exact fair conditions in return for them. If you must grant them, then I say make sure that the workers at least get a measure of the relief that you are

extending to the manufacturers. This does not imply the adoption on my part of the principle of protection. I am definitely opposed to protection as an economic principle, but I say if you feel that you must apply it, then make it mean what you say it should mean, relief to the people engaged in industry and not merely to the shareholders and the bondholders.
It is our duty as a parliament to see that in extending privileges to these industries they are carried down to the poorest worker in the plant benefiting by them; and if we fail in that duty we have failed in our responsibility as members representing the people of this country. As my hon. friend who has just taken his seat has said, we also throw into utter disrepute our whole parliamentary and political institutions. Why should industry be built up on a system of doles? That is what it means, a system of doles which you deny to the workers themselves. Better conditions, that is all we are asking for, better working conditions and a little more pay for these men. What would be the result? Better conditions would mean more efficiency; the whole history of industry is proof of that. I cannot for the life of me understand the blind greed of manufacturers who continue to employ men for ten hours and more a day. Surely they have learned the lesson that the physical ability and mental energy of the human being must and does decline after a certain number of hours of work continually performed from day to day, from week to week, from month to month and year to year. You cannot maintain a high peak of physical and mental efficiency when you are dulled by the very tedious monotony of the labour itself for almost unlimited hours.
In this connection I may refer to another fact. I wonder why, w'hen the Minister of Finance was speaking upon this subject, he did not refer to other representations which had been made before the tariff board. His attention was called to them to-night, I think, by the hon. member for North Winnipeg, and perhaps in order to bring this point clearly before the house I might just quote once more the representations made by the Ministerial Association of Sydney to the tariff board, as follows:
We recommend:
(1)	That this Ministerial Association of
Sydney wait upon the responsible heads of the D.I.S. Co. at the earliest opportunity and urge the just claims of the men for a shorter working day.	_

and when the steel companies of Canada are allowed a protective tariff that provision be made for the men receiving the standard hours of labour adopted by the parliament of Canada, namely, the eight hour day.
Now, Mr. Chairman, at this stage I think it will be fair to review very briefly one or two of the very striking statements made b3r hon. members in this debate. I find that the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Macdougall) in an eloquent appeal following the member for Winnipeg North Centre, said:
No member of this house, if he is fair, whether he is a Liberal, a Conservative, a Progressive or a Labour man, can argue that the British Empire Steel Corporation is doing what is right and fair when it compels its men to work thirteen hours a day, as they are doing in some cases, and ten hours a day as they are doing in all cases. A great many of these men do not even get one day off a week; they are compelled to work on Sunday as well.
It is almost unthinkable, Mr. Chairman, in this year and in this country that men should be working seven days a week and not less than ten hours on each of those days. The hon. member continued:
.... I believe all parties in this house, irrespective of political affiliations, should join together and say- that for once in this country we are going to place human values ahead of any other values that may be considered later. For my part I would not want one single concession made to the British Empire Steel Corporation by this government unless the government first bargained with them to give their employees a fair deal in the matter of wages and working hours.
I congratulate the hon. gentleman upon his fearless statement in that regard. He said further:
Unless the workingmen of Sydney get some benefit from these concessions, 1 am opposed to them; for any company which compels its workmen in this civilized and Christian age to work twelve hours a day and a great many of them to work seven days a week, should not be given any concessions by a civilized government.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald) then made the following

I have a practical object in view, and when the resolution comes before this house I am going to move that a provision be added that the money be not paid to the siteel company unless it shall find its way into the wage envelopes of the men.

I am a strong believer in protection to industry, but I think that protection, unless it is passed along to the worker, is repugnant to every sense of fair play.

I am not calling it a recantation or anything like that; I am calling it a slow retirement from position. He adopted the courageous position of insisting that these tariff revisions should not apply unless and until something was done for the worker, but two days later we find him receding steadily from that position. I do not know why that was done, unless this is again the little old sham battle between the two political parties when discussing tariff matters, which fact has been apparent to us for many years. I have in my hand a copy of the Scoop Shovel of May, 1930, the organ of the Manitoba wheat pool, which contains a very excellent cartoon. In the lower right hand corner is an inset circle containing a most unflattering representation of the right hon. the Prime Minister, and facing him upon a little pedestal there is portrayed the hon. leader of the opposition. Both hon. gentlemen are armed with wooden swords and carry wooden shields. They are shouting at each other at the top of their voices, but neither of them is actually striking any blows. This is labelled, "The Sham Fight." In the other part of the cartoon appears "The Real Fight," which is a fight between the profitism of protected interests and the consuming people represented by cooperation.
Put it on Hansard.

I wish I
could. That illustration on the records of the house would be well worth while. The principle we are discussing to-night is whether human life, happiness and decent living conditions are to come before or after profits. That in the final analysis is the crux of the whole discussion. I wonder whether any hon members have ever seen Millet's portrait, Man with Hoe? I am satisfied most of them have. If they have seen that picture they must have carried with them some of the thoughts I read on one occasion in a poem by Edwin Markham. I cannot remember the poem very well, but I have paraphrased and jotted down a few of the ideas. Here was the man with the hoe, and
what did we see when we looked at the picture? We saw the mark of ages of toil in the work-dulled face; we saw an expression that was dead, unlighted by any spark of active mental energy; we saw a back bent by wearisome toil. We saw neither hopelessness nor hope shining there. The weight of a world was on his shoulders, the weight of an agricultural world slowly but surely giving way, or rather, so far as the age of the world goes, speedily giving way to the new industrial age, the machine age, the mechanical age.
Had Millet lived in these days, he might have painted a different picture, the picture that we have seen of huge furnaces, blazing heat, great open plants filled with titanic energy. He might have seen in those great plants, larger than the House of Commons, little figures of men plying their tasks in front of those furnaces in a deafening, coush-ing din. He might have seen the huge white' hot ingots taken out of those furnaces and carried by overhead trolleys to the rollers where, in almost a minute as one watches, those great moltent masses of metal are rolled out into steel strips undulating like gleaming serpents later on to be turned into rigid steel. Then he might have seen the steel cut with great circular saws throwing the sparks high as a rocket burst in midair. These pictures on can see in any steel mill. You see there great cranes carrying huge electromagnets which come down and pick up four or five or more of those steel rails at one time, raise them up, a weight that it would take many men to lift, and throw them on to the racks as one would pile matches. You would see the driving ingenuity of man to save labour of man.
But has there been any change? If Millet could come and looked around him at the conditions of to-day he would find there the same type of man, the same work-dulled face hardened with dire hopelessness, with the misery and destitution of unfair exaction of labour in order that profits might come to those who own industries. Yes, he would have found men working, not as the Man with the Hoe, from sun to sun, but ten, even thirteen hours a day, for seven days a week. He would have found men working not outside in the open air and bright sunshine, but in those caverns, those huge plants with the darkening roof over them, and nothing within but the heat and stench and dust and dirt and clangor of the great machines. That is what he would have seen before him. How many years have passed since those days? I ask the house: Are we to continue to give our sanction to such conditions, or are we

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) on some of the very lofty sentiments which he has expressed to-night. Rising immediately after him I am under a great disadvantage, because it is always difficult to follow one who has within himself a monopoly of all virtue, truth, honesty of purpose, and integrity. Indeed, I could not speak after my hon. friend at all were it not for the fact that I am reminded that somewhere in the long ago a sinful man like myself went up to a certain temple to pray, and kneeling down at the door of the temple he struck his breast and said: "Mea culpa, mea culpa, mea maxima culpa." Another gentleman-probably he did not come from Bow River and perhaps he was not a Progressive; I do not know what his politics were-happened to come into the temple at the same time, and going up to the very altar rail he raised his voice on high and said: "God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are." But the funny part of it all was that Scripture records, rightly I presume, that of the two who visited the temple on that day, the man who entered at the door and confessed his sins of omission and commission went away justified.
I would point out to my hon. friend from Bow River that no matter what shade of politics we have in the house, it is a great mistake for any individual, whether he be Grit

or Tory or Progressive, to think that he and he alone has a monopoly upon sympathy so far as it extends to the labouring people of the Dominion of Canada. What I said the other night in regard to having the benefits of protection extended to the workers, I stand by now, and I remember the first speech I made in the house when, coming as I did from a labour organization, I said that any measure that might be introduced that was calculated to assist the workers, whether it was proposed by friend or political foe, would have my support. My record in that respect has been consistent. I do not stand to-night holding any brief for the British Empire Steel Corporation. I repeat that I believe it is a crying shame that the employees of the steel company at Sydney should be compelled to work ten hours and in some cases thirteen hours a day, and in some instances, seven days a week. I believe this money which is being given to the corporation by the government ought not to be given until parliament decides that those men who make the profits for the corporation shall be given at least a fair portion of that in the way of increased wages or shorter working hours.
One of the choice illogical tit-bits in the speech of my hon. friend from Bcw River who has just taken his seat, was this: With fiery denunciation he declared that protection could never assist the worker; and then in his next breath he made a long argument to show why the benefits of this protection should be applied to the steel workers of Nova Scotia.
I said that it never had protected the workers.

Then the hon. member believes that it can assist the workers, otherwise there was no reason for his speech to-night. He came to this house with all the free trade doctrines that he has imbibed, perhaps not wisely or too well, from the Manchester school, and to-night he says: Give us protection to assist the workers. He asks the government to see that the benefits from this protection shall be extended to the workers.
Hear, hear.

Then the hon. gentleman admits that protection is for the benefit of the workers of Canada. That is what the Conservative party has always stood for. I join with my hon. friend most heartily tonight in trying to see that some of the benefits resulting from application of protection in the fiscal policy of this country shall be extended to the workingmen of Nova Scotia. Protection applied, mark you, by a government

Read his speeches in Hansard; for one fortunate thing about parliament is this, that the moving finger writes and having wnt moves on, leaving its imprint upon the written page. My hon. friend to-day occupies a seat adjoining that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm), who sits in a chair protected to the extent of 42 per cent. In 1922 the Minister of Railways told us that to apply protection to the extent of 30 per cent to the boot and shoe industry in this country was protecting exploitation. It is so, and my
word is as good as my hon. friend's. Have we no longer the doctrine of cabinet solidarity in this country? During the years that have gone that principle was always maintained. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier was Prime Minister, if any cabinet minister disagreed with his policy he was discharged from the cabinet. Men were driven out of the cabinet by Laurier,- who was a man of principle, and who stuck to his principles. But to-day, sitting around the Prime Minister, we find not only the Minister of Railways but the minister who on account of his sanctimonious look was chosen a few years ago to ring the death knell of protection. Yet he swallows 400 per cent of an increase in the tariff on beans and 105 per cent of an increase in the tariff on cast iron pipe.
I say to the house that I am glad to have a convert to protection to-night in the person of my.learned and brilliant friend from Bow River, who admits that there are benefits to be derived by the workers of Canada as the result of a protective policy. I stand in this parliament to-night to say with my voice and with my vote., and I shall continue to do so
as long as it is my privilege to be in this parliament, which will be some time yet, that so far as I can see to it the benefits of the tariff shall be passed on to the steel workers of Sydney and to the workers of Canada generally wherever protection is applied, and I trust that I shall get support not only from the hon. member for Bow River but from the house generally. I trust that I shall have the support in particular of members representing the province of Nova Scotia, who are immediately concerned in this matter. The British Empire Steel Corporation is well able to take care of itself, but the men who are working long hours of labour which do not give them an opportunity for proper recreation and rest and the opportunity which they should have to educate themselves, have found from experience that they are unable to protect themselves, and therefore it is up to the members of this parliament, irrespective of party, to stand together and see that the poor men of this country get a fair deal.
Let us remember this, and I give it as a warning to all political leaders: The politics of this country in the future, as Lord Balfour said some years ago in England, will be the politics of the poor. It is the poor persons who cannot protect themselves that I want to see receiving some benefits from protection.
I trust that the house will not pass this matter over lightly, because it concerns the happiness and the standard of living of the men and women in this country who provide the purchasing power which alone is the basis on which the real progress and prosperity of this country can be built.

The resolution before the house proposes a bounty on bituminous coal mined in Canada and converted into coke in Canada and used in the smelting of iron from ore or in the production of steel. Now, Mr. Speaker, coal either alone or in the form of coke, or a combination of both, can be and is used in the smelting of iron from ore. But coke is not used in the production of steel, save in very small and negligible amounts. As drafted the bill will make available a bonus of 49J cents per ton for coal coked in Canada for the making of pig iron produced in Canada, or, say, from 721 to possibly as much as 80 cents per ton of pig iron so made. Nova Scotia steel makers are large users of Canadian coal for the production of steam, hydraulic and electric power for operating steel melting shop and other cranes. All this coal which is daily so used in steel making is by this bill entirely ignored. Again, no proper advance in duty proportioned on the additional labour involved in the various advance stages of manufacture is provided in this tariff. Further, makers of secondary products are given undue protection at the cost of the primary producers.
Due to the extended line in exemptions for duty and the free iron and steel items which are the raw material for the secondary producers, most of whose products have a fair and, indeed, some a high rate of protection, but the primary trade is unfairly dealt with.
The objectionable and most unfair former free list as here further extended in most cases where but little needed, certain favoured manufacturers thus obtaining undue protection at the expense of others who have invested immensely greater sums in plant and whose business is much more important to the state. Certainly the hon. member for Bow River took his stand on the human side of the industrial issue, and there is only one question as far as many of us are concerned with respect to industry. That is, does industry turn out better men, nobler men, cleaner men, stronger men; not does the steel industry produce greater profits or increase its output. I think the time has come when someone should lay the emphasis where it belongs, on the human side of the issue. My hon. friend from Inverness waxed eloquent on the tariff, but my hon. friend from Bow River waxed eloquent on the human interest. It was the low standard of living and the suffering of ill-paid labour which awakened the eloquence of the hon. member for Bow River.
Now let me ask the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister what they intend to do. As far as I am concerned I have no evidence that the Prime Minister is going to refuse some consideration to this question; I have no evidence that the Minister of Finance will refuse to listen to the plea which has been put forward in this connection. Indeed, I should be surprised if they did not respond, knowing them as I do, or at least knowing their viewpoint as I have heard it expressed from time to time, and knowing that they understand and respond to the human side of the question. I am not prepared to assume that they are going to turn a deaf ear to the appeal which has been made. However, let me emphasize to the Minister of Finance and to the Prime Minister that as far as I am concerned, if we are going to have protection we must make it go all round. I think it was Kant, the great philosopher, who laid down the principle that anything is wrong that you oannot universalize. If we cannot extend the principle of protection to the working classes and to the agricultural

classes, and put all classes on a basis of equality, we had better drop it altogether. I believe that something can be done in this particular instance in the interests of the working people and in the interests of the principle which I have enunciated, and I should be surprised if the leader of the opposition did not take a similar stand on this question. The party which he leads has been arguing for many years that protection does assist the working classes. Let us prove that it does by seeing that it does, and we have the opportunity here to do so.
I anticipate that if the Prime Minister refuses this request he will do so to some extent on the ground that again we shall be interfering with provincial rights, that this house has no control over the wages paid to men in certain industries, and so forth. It is the parliament of Canada which is granting to these industries the privilege of protection and parliament surely has the right to lay down conditions to the granting of that privilege. That is all we are asking the Prime Minister to do, to lay down conditions under which the protection to be extended to this industry will be available to them. We are asking that one of those conditions shall be that a fair and reasonable wage shall be paid. If anyone should ask what that means, we will refer them to the bill presented by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan). We ask that the eight hour day shall be established and that the provisions of the treaty of Versailles shall be observed. There may be technical difficulties, but it should be possible to overcome them. Personally, until I am compelled to believe it, I will not believe that either the Prime Minister or the leader of the opposition have been compelled, by any interviews with any class of people whatsoever, to recant from the position which they took a few days ago. I still have some faith in humanity, although it may have to be shaken. Once we lose our faith in humanity, nothing remains to help us along the road. In the interests of humanity I hope the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition will stretch their hands across the floor of this chamber and give a little protection to the working class to make up for what they will lose for having to pay more for their goods because of the protection proposed for the manufacturers.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be only too glad to endeavour to make clear my position. What I shall have to say about both the tariff and labour applies generally and at all times. There is a right and a wrong way to deal with any matter. There is a right way to deal with the tariff, and that is to treat all industries alike and not to discriminate with respect to any particular one. At the present time it is suggested that we deal with the tariff only as it relates to one particular industry, and as I said the other evening, we should deal either with all or with none at all. I cannot see why this house should enact tariff legislation in a manner which would single out one particular industry in one locality for one kind of treatment, and do differently with every other industry in every other locality throughout the Dominion. This parliament, I believe, would do well to adhere to the attitude which has been always adopted, namely, not to attempt to discriminate as between industry and industry, as between class and class, or as between locality and locality.

There is a right and a wong method of seeking to redress industrial wrongs. The right method is the direct method; the wrong method is to seek to do by indirect means what cannot be done by direct methods. The right method of dealing with the questions of wages and hours of labour is to deal with them in the legislatures of the provinces, which under our constitution have those questions specifically within their jurisdiction. Hon. members know very well that this parliament has no power to enact an eight hour day in any province of Canada. Hon. members who suggest we should impose an eight hour condition to any one item of our tariff legislation as respects an industry in one particular province, are seeking to do indirectly what they have no right to do directly. That is not a correct method of procedure, and I submit that in the long run we will get nowhere in this country if we attempt to deal with industrial problems in that way.
The constitution of our country clearly defines the different fields in which legislative efforts with respect to certain matters shall be put forth. So far as hours of labour, working conditions, wages and the like are concerned, the constitution of our land lays it down definitely that those are matters for provincial legislatures.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman-

The hon. member has had his say, and I should like to have the opportunity to have mine. He, amongst others, asked me to say something, and I hope he will listen to what I have to say. Some little time ago this government referred to the supreme court a question with respect to the relative jurisdictions of the federal and provincial governments in matters of this kind, and the decision of the supreme court is very pertinent to the matter under discussion at the present moment. As hon. members well know, this whole discussion arose out of a reference to the treaty of Versailles, and to the labour convention of principles associated with the League of Nations in industrial mat-

ters. That was how the question first came up for discussion in reference to the tariff generally, and more specifically in reference to the bill regarding the so-called bonus.
The five cent piece.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was this
very matter of obligation as between the federal anid the provincial governments arising out of the treaty of Versailles which was referred to the supreme court. I have in my hand the opinion which was given by the Supreme Court of Canada in this matter. It may be well for me to place it on Hansard because it will go very far towards clearing up some of the confusion which has been created in the course of this debate.
On January 12, 1925, the reference to which I refer was made by an order in council of the Dominion government of certain questions as to the obligations of Canada arising out of the Labour part of the treaties of Peace, and also as to the legislative authority of the Dominion parliament or of the provincial legislatures to deal with a certain draft convention which had been adopted by the International Labour Conference (League of Nations) in 1919, limiting the hours of work in industries to eight in the day and forty-eight in the week. The judgment of the court was delivered on June 11, 1925, and it was unanimous. In effect it is a confirmation of the view which was expressed by the law officers of the crown and embodied in an order in council of the Dominion government adopted in November, 1920.
The judgment of the court was in the terms following:-
In the matter of a reference by His Excellency the Governor General in Council to the Supreme Court of Canada of certain questions relating to legislative jurisdiction over hours of labour.
The very question we are discussing at the moment.
The judgment of the court-the Chief Justice and Duff, Mignault, Rinfret, and Magee J.J.-was delivered by Duff J.-
The first of the questions submitted concerns the general effect of one of the clauses in Artcile 405 of the Treaty of Versailles and the corresponding provision in the other treaties of peace. This article is one of those comprised in the labour part (part 13) of the treaties and it defines the undertaking entered into by each of the members respecting recommendations and draft conventions adopted by the general conference of representatives of the members of the League of Nations established as part of a permanent organization for the promotion of the objects set forth in the preamble to that part. The pertinent clause is in these words:-
"Each of the members undertakes that it will, within the period of one year at most

from the closing of the session of the conference, or if it is impossible owing to exceptional circumstances to do so within the period of one year, then at the earliest practical moment and in no case later than eighteen months from the closing of the session of the conference bring the recommendation or draft conyention before the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies, for the enactment or legislation or other action."
It seems very clear that the duty arising under this clause is not a duty to enact legislation or to promote legislation; it is an undertaking simply to bring the recommendation or draft convention before the competent authority No question is submitted as to the duty of the member arising under the succeeding clauses of the same article in the event of the competent authority or authorities giving its or their consent to the recommendation or draft convention; and upon this no opinion is expressed.	,
The second, third and fourth questions submitted relate to a particular draft convention; that, namely, adopted by the general conference of the international Labour Organization of the League of Nations on the 29th of October. 1919, which has for its object the limiting of the hours of work in industrial undertakings as therein defined to eight hours in the day and forty-eight hours m the week.
Under the scheme of distribution ot legislative authority in the British North America Act. legislative jurisdiction touching the subject' matter of this convention is, subject to a qualification to be mentioned, primarily vested in the provinces. Under the head of jurisdiction numbered 13 in section 92, Property and Civil Rights, or under the sixteenth head, Local and Private Matters Within the Province, or under both heads, each of the provinces possesses authority to give the force of law in the province to provisions such as those contained in the draft convention. This general proposition is subject to this qualification, namelv that as a rule a province has no authority to regulate the hours of employment of the servants of the Dominion government.
It seems questionable whether government employees, in industrial undertakings carried on by the government, such, for example, as shipbuilding, are within the scope of the convention. The point was not the subject ot argument before us, and concerning it no opinion in intended to be expressed.
It is necessary to observe, also, that as regards those parts of Canada which are not included within the limits of any province, the legislative authority in relation to civil rights generally, and to the subject matter of the convention in particular, is the Dominion parliament.
Then a little further down:
It follows from what has been said that the draft convention ought to be brought before the parliament of Canada as being the competent legislative authority for those parts of Canada not within the boundaries of any province; and if servants of the Dominion government engaged in industrial undertakings as defined by the convention are within the scope of its provisions, then the Dominion parliament is the competent authority also to give force of law to those provisions as applicable to such persons.
The convention should also be brought before the lieutenant-governor of each of the provinces for the purpose of enabling him to bring it to the attention of the provincial legislature as possessing, subject to the qualification mentioned, legislative jurisdiction within the province in relation to the subject matter of the convention.
The judgment continues to give answers to the several questions as indicated. I submit that that judgment is a guide as to the correct method of procedure to those who are interested in industrial matters, particularly to those who seek the improvement of conditions under which labour is working in our country. Where the matter is one that comes within the jurisdiction of the Dominion, let us by all means seek to the extent of our power to see that the principles associated with the League of Nations are carried out under federal jurisdiction. That is what the government has done in larger measure at this session than has been done at any previous time. We have in the supplementary estimates which have been brought down an item with respect to employees in only one department of the public service, amounting, as far as I am able to recall at the moment, to something like $667,000. I am not sure that in the supplementary estimates which were laid on the table last night more than $1,000,000 is not being asked of parliament for the sole purpose of -making possible the carrying out of the eight-hour day principle in its application to classes of labour or service controlled by the Dominon.

What does that provision mean? It means that this government stands foursquare in its intention, to the extent of its power, not indirectly, not by some subterfuge, but directly, out in the open, in a straightforward way, to do all it can to ensure that the principles associated with the League of Nations with respect to industrial conditions and labour are carried out. Where those principles relate to matters coming within the jurisdiction of the provinces, we say that if a province will notify us that there is any industry within their jurisdiction which is receiving aid from the federal treasury and which is not complying in any particular with any law which it has passed for the purpose of carrying out principles associated with the League of Nations-the eight hour day, the minimum wage, the fair wage, or any of those conditions-we will withhold whatever is being given that industry from the federal treasury.
I ask, can there be a more effective way of dealing with these matters?
We are discussing at the moment one particular concern, but these laws are made for all concerns which may to-day or hereafter come to foe applicable under them. So far as the industry which has been particularly referred to is concerned, the British Empire Steel Corporation, I believe it is true that that industry has recently been considerably reorganized. I know a good deal about labour conditions in that industry in previous years. I have had something to do with seeking to bring about better conditions in that industry during a period of twenty or thirty years. I have followed the progress of that industry with a good deal of personal 
interest and concern. I believe it is true that to-day that industry comes nearer to being on its feet, so to speak, in a legitimate way than it has been at any time since its inception. At this moment the men employed in that industry as well as those who have capital invested in it are looking forward hopefully to seeing that industry become established, under fair conditions, in the province of Nova Scotia. Now it may take very little to have that hope realized; it may take equally little altogether to destroy it. What we as a government are seeking to do is to follow the direction given to us by the commission on maritime claims which investigated conditions in Nova Scotia, and which made certain recommendations with respect to what they believe should be done for the iron and steel industry and the coal industry in that province in order to give them their fair chance. His reply to me was that before the company paid out anything in the way of dividends it would be seen that the bonus had helped to improve the conditions of labour, that I might expect to see that before dividends were declared the conditions of labour would be still further improved over what they are at the present time.

proving the conditions of their workmen, in the matter of wages and in the matter of hours, if I am in the place in the government of this country which I occupy at the moment, I will seek to do my part to see that any assistance that is being given by this government is withheld until some action is taken along the right line.

Perhaps the Prime
Minister would tell us what the British Empire Steel Corporation did with the million dollars profit which they made on steel last year. Did they apply that to giving better wages or shorter hours to their workmen?

We have heard it said over and over again in this debate that money should not be paid as dividends to the shareholders until something was done to improve the conditions of labour. With that I agree entirely, but I say that the way to go about effecting that result so far as parliament is concerned, is to proceed in accordance with a method that is not open to question, and which in the long -run is certain ta bring about the best results.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up further time. AH I desire to make clear is this, that so far as Canada is concerned it is a country made up of nine provinces, each with its own government, having jurisdiction with regard to certain matters and this federal parliament to deal with other matters. One of the most serious problems continually confronting us, it seems to me, is to maintain on an even, fair and just basis the relations between the respective provinces and the Dominion, and any efforts that are made, so far as this Dominion government is concerned, to encroach upon the field of the provinces in matters of legislation, or efforts made to coerce the provinces by indirect methods, will not help in the long run, nor will they 6erve to maintain the structure of confederation as it is to-day. I say, Mr. Speaker, that by each of us in our own field doing the best we can, we will in the end do more for those we are seeking to help than by any other method.
I would say to my hon. friends who have spoken so eloquently and so feelingly on this matter to-night that I hope they will at the earliest opportunity go and repeat the speeches which they have made in this house to the government of Nova Scotia, to the members of that government who have it within their power at this minute-

If they will pass that eight hour law or any law in respect of wages which is based upon the labour convention of the Versailles treaty or the principles associated with the League of Nations, and will tell us that that law is not being observed by a company that is being aided by moneys from the treasury of this country, and the governor in council has reason to be satisfied that such is the case, then I say from that moment further assistance will be withheld until the law is observed.

Mr. Chairman, I
regret exceedingly that the Prime Minister has taken the stand that he has taken to-night. Once again he has sought refuge behind the British North America Act. Further than that, it seems to me that the statement he has made has tended to obscure the real issue before the house. The judgment of the supreme court, which was read at length and with which we are familiar, deals with legislative authority. No one is proposing to draft legislation here to-night. We know perfectly well that under the decision of the supreme court we cannot draft such legislation. Some of us may doubt whether the decisions of the supreme court might not ultimately be reversed, but so long as they stand we will accept the position for the purpose of this argument that we cannot draft such legislation.
But, Mr. Chairman, none of us to-night is proposing that, none of us is asking the government to do that. What we are asking the government to do is altogether a different matter and one which comes entirely within the jurisdiction of this parliament. What we find to-day is a request from these corporations for special privileges, and what we do say is that in granting special privileges the grantor has a perfect right to lay down the conditions under which they shall be granted. The Prime Minister says that in the future if the company does not live up to the undertaking which they have given to him he will find means to make them do so. Why not find such means now? Some of us have watched these deplorable conditions for a good many years. I have known these conditions to exist during the nine years I have been in this house, and we have seen no amelioration of them. We

have had during that time strike upon strike; we have had the military sent down again and again to this district to quell labour troubles; we have had commission after commission go down and report. The Duncan commission report is to be implemented, we are told, because it deals with the relief of the industry; but the other reports are not to be implemented. No, they deal only with the relief of the men who work.
The Prime Minister says that wages and hours of labour should be dealt with by the province. I say as far as legislation is concerned let us concede that. But we have a great many precedents under which we as a parliament may have something to say with regard to wages, working hours and so on. For expamle, when we give a contract we stipulate what wages and hours shall govern, whether the contractor lives in Nova Scotia or British Columbia; that is one case in which we deal with wages and hours-not by legislation, but by regulation, because we are dealing with matters that come under our own jurisdiction. In the same way in the granting of certain licences we determine the conditions under which those licences shall be granted, and it is conceded that we have a perfect right to deal with such matters even though they relate to wages and working hours. We are not putting legislation on the statute books; we are exercising powers vested in this government in relation to the granting of such licences. The same thing applies on the incorporation of a private concern; again and again in the past few years in the case of certain international bridges we have inserted in the charters a fair wage clause, even though these structures authorized were situated in the province of Ontario on one bank of the river and in New York state on the other bank. There again it was not a matter of legislation, but we said: Since these companies come to us asking for incorporation, we have a perfect right to state the conditions under which that incorporation shall be granted. I do not think I need continue to give further precedents along that line.
The Prime Minister says that we must not coerce the provinces. I want to suggest that in this very tariff we have in the past again and again coerced outside bodies. We have even coerced, if you like to put it that way, the empire itself, because we have insisted that there shall be a certain empire content of material and labour in their manufactured goods or else they cannot be imported under the preferential tariff. If you talk of coercion in that sense, I say we are coercing the empire by insisting on certain conditions with which

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
their manufactured goods must comply. We do no more here. We say: Before this tariff is applicable the industries must come up to a certain standard. That is not legislation, and I do not think the Prime Minister will seriously state that the supreme court decided anything which touches upon this matter at all.
The Prime Minister says that it is not fair to deal with one particular industry, that any legislation should deal with all industries. Possibly that may be correct in theory, but we have pointed out again and again that this particular industry is the only industry in Canada which is working a considerable body of its men eleven and thirteen hours a day. We are not concerned with the other industries that are working their men only eight hours a day; perhaps we are not even concerned with those that are working their men ten hours a day, although that is longer than the hours prescribed by the Versailles treaty. But we are trying to find some means of curbing these corporations that are working their men eleven' and thirteen hours a day and seven days a week. And so I say we have to deal with a particular industry, and there is nothing wrong in dealing with that industry when it is the industry that is sinning in this regard.
Further than that it is this particular industry that is seeking this special protection. We are dealing with a special item of the tariff. I would point out to the Prime Minister that some industries are protected to the extent of 10 or 15 or 20 per cent, some to the extent of 30 and 40 per cent; surely we have discrimination between industries. Some industries such as farming, are not protected at all. Surely this is discrimination. Surely the very complexity of our tariff schedules shows discrimination. So when it is stated that we must not discriminate against one industry, again I say we are elaborating a theoretical principle which in practice does not exist. In taking action along this line we are simply doing something which we are doing every day when we put through any of these tariff items.
The Prime Minister has brought forward as the only one contribution that the government is prepared to make in regard to this whole matter a section in the bill before the house, an act to place Canadian coal used in the manufacture of iron and steel on a basis of equality with imported coal. That section would contain a condition that before this bonus is given there should be certain conditions complied with. If the government of the 2419-1704
province of Nova Scotia or any other government enacted the eight hour day it would have to be complied with. That may sound well, and it may look well on paper, but it is not worth the paper upon which it is written. Hon. members in this house know very well that the British Empire Steel Corporation practically controls the province of Nova Scotia. We know that since the Versailles treaty this government, in the performance of its duty, has asked the province of Nova Scotia to inaugurate an eight hour working day, and that province so far has refused to do so. There is no particular reason to hope that in the near future the attitude of the province of Nova Scotia will change. Under these conditions we are simply putting in a dead letter clause; that is all that this government is offering to help the situation.
I do not want to prolong this debate, but we in this corner of the house are honest in our contentions, and I think that some who have claimed honesty will permit us to say that we have introduced this matter in the hope that we may secure some alleviation for the conditions under which the steel workers find themselves. I am not concerned with the factional disputes over the items contained in the tariff, but I am concerned in getting better conditions for these labouring men. I had hoped that this government, which has claimed again and again to be the friend of the workers, would solve my problem, but it has failed to do so. At this particular stage of the proceedings I believe it is out of order to offer a resolution, but at a later stage when we are in a position to discuss the bill which I understand is to follow, we propose to move an amendment. It may be that we in this corner of the house are too weak to pass such an amendment; certainly we cannot carry it by ourselves, but I am hoping that a considerable number of gentle-ment to my right will come to our assistance, and it may be that there are some hon. members across the floor of the house who will lend their aid. We purpose to move an amendment to the effect that these tariff privileges will be given only when the industry producing the articles has demonstrated to the satisfaction of the governor in council that in the operation of such industry employees are being paid a fair and reasonable wage, and that there has been instituted an eight hour day and a forty-eight hour week in accordance with the conditions of the Washington labour conference held under the authority of the treaty of Versailles. If we are successful in passing an amendment of that nature we will bring immediate relief

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
to these steel workers. When the government intends to give special privileges which will mean the placing of larger amounts of money into the hands of the British Empire Steel Corporation I see no reason why we should not insist that such privileges should be granted conditionally upon the workers being paid a decent wage and living under decent conditions.

My hon. friend knows
very well that I respect him; we are two members in this house who suffer most through our allegiance to truth and principle. He makes the suggestion that he will propose an amendment, but may I remind him that his proposed amendment is ultra vires of the jurisdiction of this parliament. He wants to help the miners, but if his amendment is ultra vires and is declared null and void by the courts, it will not be much help to the miners.

In the first place, I am not talking about the miners; I am talking about steel workers. If what I have said does not show that my amendment in the miners' interests is intra vires, nothing I can say will help.

I wish to make a few observations in connection with this matter. I think that the Prime Minister and my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre both have the same object in view; they are working in the interests of the workers in the steel industry. As to the constitutional powers of this parliament to impose conditions upon tariff increases I regret that I must differ from the opinion expressed by my leader, the Prime Minister, and must agree with the sentiments of my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre. In my opinion it is within the jurisdiction of this parliament to impose such conditions as it might consider reasonable upon any tariff changes which are made in this parliament. We have full jurisdiction over the tariff and we have the right to impose any conditions we desire with regard to tariffs or the changing of tariffs. That is my opinion as to the constitutional powers of this parliament, and I can see no reason whatever why it would not be within our jurisdiction to impose such a condition as has been suggested by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre. The rules of the house preclude any amendment by a private member at this stage, but if my hon. friend will bring in his suggested amendment to the bill when it is in committee I shall be glad to vote for it.

Hear, hear.

speechtext: When the committee rose we were considering item 377c.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that there are some things I should like to say in regard to the item under discussion. When one listens to the righteously indignant speech of the Prime Minister one is convinced of what one often hears, that he has a flair for waxing righteously indignant when that particular method is required. Indeed, the Prime Minister, who has time and again said that he was the friend of the worker, and who is now in the position of defending legislation brought forward for the benefit of a special privilege group without at the same time guaranteeing that part of that special privilege for which all the people in Canada pay will be passed on to the worker, has every need for a flair for righteous indignation. I do not forget the conditions of the steel workers as I saw them when I visited Nova Scotia in 1925. These men and women live as none of us want to live; as we would not want any of our people to live, as our hardworking farmers who work more than twelve hours a day live. They do need whatever help we can give them, and I support most heartily what has been said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
After all, it is the business of the Dominion parliament to look after the people of Canada and not after the specially privileged groups in Canada. Surely the people in the country soon ought to come to realize what has been true for some time in Canada, that special privilege groups work under the mantles of the two great political parties. When the Prime Minister hurls-particularly at the hon. member for Bow River but after all at all of us in this comer-the suggestion that we are giving ourselves a righteousness that does not

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
belong to us, we can say to him that we are at least quite honestly and clearly and above board a class group, and we are not ashamed of it. We do not hide it under a mantle with a general name, and it does seem to me perfectly clear that under the mantle of so-called great Liberal principles, special privilege groups are being well looked after and that the welfare of the workers in this particular matter is not being looked after at all.
I am sorry to disappoint the Prime Minister. While I admire the cleverness with which he made his speech and the vigour which came to him-one might almost say the eloquence-I am afraid it falls on deaf ears in this corner. We have heard the same kind of thing for a long time without seeing results follow.

The question which has been going through my mind ever since the proposal was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was whether his proposition was practicable and whether it would be possible for a minister of national revenue, entrusted with the administration of an act containing such a provision, to administer that are. I listened with a great deal of interest to the very eloquent speech made by the hon. member for Bow River, and I should be very loath to do anything that would seem for a moment to underestimate the importance of this matter from the humanitarian standpoint; but we are here this evening dealing with a question which we must consider not from the theoretical standpoint only but from the standpoint also of whether or not the proposition is practicable.
With what the hon. member for Bow River said in regard to tariffs in general I am in hearty accord, and if he takes the position that these particular duties are wrong in themselves, I am willing to agree with him most heartily. However, when he takes the position that these tariffs must be levied only on consideration that certain conditions be observed by the Besco Company, and advances that as a practical proposition, I must say that I dissent. He referred to the words of the leader of the opposition, when he said:
Here we have a chance to say that these increases shall apply only to such mills as maintain the principles of the treaty of Versailles.
I should like the hon. member for Bow River or those who are supporting him in this matter to point out how it is possible to mlake the benefits of tariff legislation apply only to certain companies in this country. Tariff legislation must be general in its scope; it cannot possibly be made to apply to the
Besco Company and not apply to another steel company which possibly may be observing the terms of the treaty of Versailles in regard to the eight hour day.
With me this is a practical proposition; how can it be done? It would seem to me rather inconsiderate of the hon. member for Bow River to recall the words of the leader of the opposition. The hon. gentleman has the sometimes fatal gift of fluency in language, and sometimes I think his words run ahead of his thoughts. I believe that on more mature consideration the leader of the opposition would admit that the proposal involved in the sentence quoted is absolutely impracticable. This is the question which concerns me at the moment, Mr. Chairman: How is it possible, under tariff legislation which must be general in its scope, to make it apply to only such a branch of the industry or to such a company engaged in the particular industry as observes certain conditions? If it were a matter of a bonus to a particular manufacturer, then we might impose that Obligation, but how it can be done under tariff legislation is a mystery to me. I hope those who have indicated their intention to bring forward an amendment at a later date will consider it from this standpoint and not be content with general expressions of opinion, not say merely that the thing is theoretically sound, is desirable from the humanitarian standpoint, but also show how it possibly can be done and how the Minister of National Revenue, in carrying out the act, will be able to do it in accordance with the wishes expressed by hon. members themselves.
I express this hope, that when the time comes to, move that amendment, as I understand my hon. friends intend to do, they will show that the proposal is practicable. Otherwise I am afraid I shall have to vote against it, as I would feel disposed to do at the present time.

The observations made
by the right hon. Prime Minister more fittingly illustrate the difficulties of disregarding principles than anything I have heard for some time. He says that we must never forget the relative rights, constitutionally, of the provinces, and that to impose conditions upon provinces might be and is highly improper, if not illegal.
We are not imposing any conditions upon the provinces.

At the moment I am
addressing my remarks to the committee; I was referring to the observations of the right
2694	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
hon. Prime Minister and not to those of his deputy. May I observe that the legislation which was adopted by this bouse on a previous occasion at the instance of the Prime Minister and his government disregarded that principle? It will be recalled that the premier of Quebec, Mr. Taschereau, has indicated that he has had the opinion of two eminent lawyers to the effect that the action taken by this parliament on that occasion was illegal. We provided for the granting of old age pensions by the provinces, and stated that we would pay half of the money, but we imposed conditions under which we would pay it. Those conditions were imposed upon the provinces whether they did or did not like them; if they accepted the principle they accepted the conditions. This parliament, at the instance of the Prime Minister and his government, imposed upon the various provinces which accepted the old age pensions scheme, a plan which provided conditions under which they could obtain the benefits; if they did not want the benefits, they did not accept the scheme. The scheme contained conditions with which every hon. member of this house is familiar; the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre knows quite well what they were.
Let us analyze the proposal to see whether it be sound or unsound from the point of view of the constitution. Undoubtedly parliament has the jurisdiction to deal with the tariff; in fact it is the only legislative body in Canada which can deal with that matter. The tariff which existed before the present tariff bill was introduced had existed for many years, and under it and by virtue of reorganization the institution mentioned had grown to a position, as the Prime Minister said, which was better than ever before attained in its history. That being so, a special concession is being given to that organization because of the recommendations of the Duncan report.

The only question to which I directed my mind the other evening was whether or not we had a legal right to impose conditions, and I agree with the hon. gentleman from Winnipeg in the view he has expressed in that regard.
Leaving that for the moment, we then consider the matter of an amendment. I do not think there is any doubt that an amendment moved by a private member of this house would be out of order, because it would be interfering with a plan or scheme of finance introduced by the minister. When I made inquiry the other afternoon the clerk of the house satisfied me in that regard. The Deputy Speaker has ruled out of order a certain amendment in that direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not say that it would be out of order at a later stage.

I gathered from the quotation from May which the Chairman read, that that would be the case. However, I am not certain about that, but it has nothing to do with the point I am endeavouring to make. I ventured to point out the other evening that parliament, in my judgment, has the power to adopt this course of action. I made also a very strong statement with respect to the eighty-four hour week. However, any man is entitled to search for information, and in answer to the question raised by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) I should like to associate myself with the right hon. the Prime Minister in stating that anyone should be entitled to ask for information without being suspected of improper motives.
I asked information of certain gentlemen who I thought would be able to inform me.
The making of steel is a continuous process; it is not a question of an eight hour day, it is a question of shifts. There must be either two or three; if three, they would be of eight hours each, if two, they would be divided into two twelve hour shifts or one thirteen and one eleven hour shift. I have been advised, and I have seen the process

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
myself, that the work itself is not continuous. Between the opening of the furnace in order to allow the metal to pour out there are certain periods of rest which make the actual hours of labour much less than has been indicated. I have been informed that under modern practice the use of pneumatic tools eases the actual labour to a considerable extent, and the conditions are not as bad as I was led to believe.
Three years ago the system was changed in some of the plants in the United States from two shifts to three, but up to date all the plants have not been able to adopt that new system. This change involves an expenditure of from $200,000 to $300,000 for a moderately small plant, and the reasons given by those responsible for the management of this enterprise for their inability to adopt the new method is that the company is only recently out of a receivership, and the solution as to how they would be able to attain this end has not been arrived at. As I understand it, they have given to the Prime Minister an undertaking that no dividends will be paid upon the capital stock of the enterprise in its reorganized condition unless and until an improvement in working conditions has been provided for those who create the profits out of which the dividends can be paid. Speaking for myself, I am disposed to say that an enterprise which has been in the hands of a receiver as long as this one has been, and which has met with the difficulties encountered by this one, should be given an opportunity-not a long one-to determine whether or not it is possible to attain to the condition which now obtains in the United States Steel Corporation and other plants in the United States.
It is not a question of an eight hour day, but rather one of eight hour shifts, because steel making being a continuous process it is necessary that workmen should be there prepared at all times to do the work. However, I am informed that these men do not work continuously for an eighty-four hour week; they work six days out of the week and have one day in seven of rest. If the furnaces are operated on Sunday it is necessary that some men work on that day, but they receive another iday of rest during the week. That is the practice which obtains at the present time in the larger plants. What the bon. member for Winnipeg North Centre hao said as to its being advisable from the standpoint of the proprietors has, I think, been abundantly established by the results which have been obtained in certain plants. In view of the information which I have received that some 25,000 men are employed in this enterprise, one has to consider whether or not the promise given steadily to improve conditions until there are three shifts instead of two, should be substituted at this moment for any legislative action. If this were my own property to be dealt with under the circumstances, I would endeavour to see to^ what extent good faith would be accepted in the promise made by the Prime Minister. That is the way it would strike me at the moment.
The hon. member for Bow River and others have referred to the fact that in days gone by the party with which I am associated has indicated that the protection of the workingman is of fundamental importance. I think they have hardly put the matter fairly. We say' that industry can be developed in this country only if it is afforded an opportunity to compete on even terms with industry in other countries. That involves a consideration of rates of pay, hours of labour, cost of raw materials and everything that is a factor in cost of production. But may I add this: the only reason that tariffs are regarded as being of value in that respect is that without tariffs there can be no industry in Canada -let us face that frankly-and there must be a tariff until industry in our own country has attained to such a strength and position that it can compete with industry in other countries. No one in Canada learned that more quickly than the farmer in respect to the New Zealand treaty, and he learned it to his sorrow. No one has learned it better than the bean producers, who have the benefit of the tariff placed on their product at the present session. It was a Liberal government led by a free trade Minister of Finance who placed upon the tariff books of this country for the protection of the bean grower a provision amounting to an increase of something like 200 per cent over the old duty rate.

Three hundred per
cent.
The rate being four times as much and the increase being 300 per cent.

Five hundred per
cent.

I am glad to see that
my hon. friends are now thinking in terms of hundreds per cent increases in order that they may justify their action to their constituents. They no longer are the party of free trade. They have now become the party of increase in tariffs by hundreds per cent.
The question in this case is purely as to how and when the end can best be accomplished, having regard to the number of people employed and the necessity for some
