protection. Protection is not primarily for capital; it is in order that there may be any industry at all in this country that we asked for it in the first instance. We ask for it not as an expedient, not as a deathbed repentance just before an election, but as a principle; when we had no election pending we asked for it from one session to another. Everyone has now adopted it; in the case of my hon. friends opposite not as a principle but as an expedient, and in our case as a continuing principle. I put this to the house: Would there be in this country any industry of any kind in the steel business without some protection? If there would not be, then obviously the tariff ensures employment, and as it ensures employment it therefore is a protection for labour; because it means that labour can stay in Canada and not have to migrate to some other country in order to secure a job.
I could give instance after instance. The hon. member for Bow River referred to the textile industry. The other day I was given the names of nine woollen mills in Ontario that are closed and the number of spindles in those mills that are idle because they no longer have an opportunity to compete on even terms with the mills of other countries. I went to Sherbrooke, to the great Paton plant, and I found there the spindles idle because of the tariff enacted in this house. The manager did not hesitate to say: You can come and look at the machines and the men; there is the list of workmen employed; there is the diminution of the number because of the tariff enacted in parliament. I went to another plant and I found there the same condition.
I give these instances because I desire to point out how unfair are the statements that have been made in the house this afternoon. Protection is a principle that, applied to Canada, means that we have an opportunity to develop our industrial life. Unless we have that we cannot develop; for as long as this country is the slaughter market for the surplus mass production of our great neighbour to the south, there can be no industrial life and consequently no general employment in Canada. That, it seems to me, is the whole reason behind the effort to apply the principle of protection-and the government has now adopted that principle-to the fiscal life of the country. Of course, if this country develops as we believe it will, the necessity for the protection should become less. As the industry strengthens, the necessity for supporting it correspondingly diminishes, and there is no doubt, despite what my hon. friend from

Rosetown will say, that the principle enunciated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce is true, namely, that if the domestic industry has the domestic market there will be such competition as to ensure that there will be no increase in prices by reason of communities outside of Canada not being permitted on unfair terms to compete with Canadian industry.
A manufacturer pointed out to me a year ago that if the tariff on his product could be increased 10 per cent, he would reduce his prices by 10 per cent because the volume of his business would be increased accordingly. That has been the history of the United States -volume of business decreasing unit overhead cost and the decreasing of unit overhead cost meaning, of course, a lessening of prices. The point that the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen made in dealing with the problem is that in the mind of every Canadian legislator there is the idea that in giving the necessary encouragement to the development of industry in Canada we should take the essential steps to protect the consumer from exploitation; in other words, that the domestic competition, to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce referred, is ensured in order that there be such active demand for the products produced in our own country that the price will not be out of line with what it would be for the imported article. It does not follow that the price in the domestic market is the price in the foreign country plus the protection. The duty may be high enough to shut out the commodity altogether. Then it becomes necessary for parliament so to legislate as to ensure the Consumer against exploitation while supplying an opportunity for labour on the part of our own Canadian people. There can be employment in this country only if we afford the opportunity, and I agree with my hon. friend -and I believe those who have been before me in this position have always enunciated the same view whether in office or out of office -that the application of that principle to the fiscal life of the country is not only for the purpose of developing Canadian life, of affording opportunities for employment to Canadians in Canada, of encouraging the building of homes in Canada, of creating of stable conditions in Canada, but of providing a living wage for men who toil and giving them in addition some opportunity for leisure and the improvement of their homes and family life so that they may become good and useful citizens of this Dominion.
I firmly believe that unless that principle is applied, the end aimed at cannot be attained. Aiming at that end, as we do in Nova Scotia

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
and other parts of the Dominion, I believe an opportunity should be afforded to those who have given their solemn assurance to the Prime Minister that they will endeavour to bring about that purpose, to see whether or not they can eSectuate it; and if with the facilities which the government has at its command those purposes are not effectuated by the efforts of those concerned, then indeed the parliament that grants is the parliament that can repeal.
I have not changed a single thought that I expressed the other evening with respect to a matter of this kind. In view of what was said to me I did make inquiries; I invited an opportunity to ask questions of gentlemen whose words I accept as being true, and the assurance which the Prime Minister was given is an assurance which was given also to myself. I have reason to believe that unless that assurance is implemented by effort, and in the end by results commensurate with the promise given, parliament will not be slow to indicate its views in the premises.
Those are my convictions, which I have no hesitation in expressing to this house because I do not conceive it possible for Canada to make any progress in industry and in the development of our vast resources unless we aim to protect those who toil with their hands as well as those who risk their capital iD enterprise. The first consideration must be for those who toil; for they have a more difficult task and are less able to look after their own interests. Capital may seek employment elsewhere usefully and profitably, whereas those who live in our own country can never migrate without grave inconvenience to themselves and the disruption of their homes. It is for these reasons that I venture at this time to say, in connection with the statement made by the Prime Minister, that he applied an entirely different principle in dealing with the problem of old age pensions. It is competent for parliament at all times to impose any condition it pleases upon legislation that it enacts, and granting that those conditions may be imposed, the only question is whether or not that power should be exercised to-day or to-morrow; if to-morrow, then only because waiting until then affords an opportunity to ascertain whether or not, having regard to the complexity of modern industry, the competition that exists, and the difficulties that have been experienced in establishing a stable industry, the assurances given are capable of being implemented to the full.

I did not intend to enter into this debate, but seeing that the house is not disposed to let this measure go through, I will add a word or two. We seem to be enacting over again the old scene which was enacted some thirty years or more ago when these same companies got every concession possible, tariffs, bonuses, and special privileges, to establish an industry down there by the sea. We are no nearer the establishment of a steel industry in Canada to-day than we were when Sir Wilfrid Laurier bonused the Dominion Iron and Steel Company for that very purpose, and our efforts to-day are just as futile as they were then. The tariff has never yet established any industry. There is no industry, according to my friends on the protectionist benches, that is any nearer making its own way to-day than it was forty years ago.
I am sorry that the Prime Minister has thrown out a kind of a challenge to-night to this corner of the house, accusing us of insinuations regarding this tariff question. I have heard before these old promises of having protection extended to other classes. In fact some thirty or more years ago it was a common thing to hear from one end of this Dominion to the other the statement that the workingman was going to get a cosy home and a full dinner pail, and so on; yet after all the billions of dollars that have been spent in the establishment of these industries we are not any nearer that objective than we were thirty years ago, and the conditions of the workingmen in some of our industries cannot be compared with those which prevail in any other country on the northern hemisphere. In fact I believe our workingmen are in a more precarious condition as to their living and employment than the workingmen in England. If we did throw out insinuations, we are in mighty good company. Let me quote from the words of the present leader of the opposition, speaking on this very subject some years ago. He said:
I appeal to every man in this house and say that if he will take the time to read the history of the operations of Mackenzie and Mann from that time till now, he will find nothing but a long trail of parliamentary corruption, of lobbying of degradation of parliamentary institutions, of the lowering of the morale of public life and the degrading of those standards by which public life should be truly measured. Both sides of the house have been to blame. Look to the statute books for the aid that has been given to this company.
